stories.title: Crew-13 reaches the space station in 7 hours 55 minutes, the fastest trip ever for a U.S. spacecraft
stories.summary: SpaceX’s Crew-13 mission for NASA docked with the International Space Station on Oct. 1, just 7 hours and 55 minutes after launching from Florida. NASA officials said it was the fastest any American spacecraft has ever reached the orbiting lab.
stories.summaryLong:
SpaceX’s Crew-13 mission for NASA arrived at the International Space Station on Thursday, Oct. 1, at 7:05 p.m. EDT—7 hours and 55 minutes after it launched from Florida’s Space Coast. NASA officials said that is the fastest any American spacecraft has ever reached the orbiting lab.

The previous record for a U.S. vehicle was 12 hours and 33 minutes, set in November 2024 by SpaceX’s Dragon cargo capsule on the robotic CRS-31 resupply flight. The fastest astronauts had made the trip in a U.S. vehicle was 14 hours and 43 minutes, achieved by the Crew-11 mission in August 2025.

“We got lucky this time,” Julianna Scheiman, SpaceX’s director of NASA science and Dragon programs, said at the post-launch press conference. “The space station was in an opportune spot in space, and the orbital mechanics, the physics of it all, worked out for it to be the shortest launch-to-docking time we’ve had to date,” she said, adding that “this is close to the fastest it could be.”

Crew-13 did not set the overall speed record to the station—a Russian Soyuz carrying three astronauts once reached the lab just 3 hours and 3 minutes after liftoff. Space.com notes the Soyuz isn’t faster or more powerful than a Dragon; the difference comes mainly from mission controllers choosing more aggressive “fast-track” trajectories.

Crew-13 delivered four astronauts: NASA’s Jessica Watkins and Luke Delaney, Joshua Kutryk of the Canadian Space Agency and Sergey Teteryatnikov of Roscosmos. The quartet will live and work in space for the next six months, relieving the four members of Crew-12—NASA astronauts Jessica Meir and Jack Hathaway, ESA’s Sophie Adenot and cosmonaut Andrey Fedyaev—who launched in mid-February and are preparing to return to Earth in their Crew Dragon capsule.
stories.whyMatters: A smooth, record-quick handoff keeps four new crew members working on the station for six months.

stories.title: Greater Portland’s Metro reaches 20,000 acres of protected parks and natural areas
stories.summary: Metro’s portfolio of parks, natural areas, trails and historic cemeteries has hit 20,000 acres, a milestone more than three decades in the making. Voters funded it through three parks-and-nature bonds and a levy, and the land protects salmon habitat and drinking water for hundreds of thousands of people.
stories.summaryLong:
This year, Metro, greater Portland’s regional government, is celebrating a major conservation milestone: its portfolio of green spaces has reached 20,000 acres. It started with a few thousand acres transferred from Portland and Multnomah County in the early 1990s and has grown into a network of parks, natural areas, regional trails and historic cemeteries meant to protect the region’s water quality and natural beauty.

Metro didn’t do it alone. Voters across the region passed three parks and nature bonds that funded land purchases and passed and renewed a levy that supports ongoing care. Other agencies, community organizations and tribal governments helped set priorities, and property owners chose to sell or donate land for nature.

The stories behind the map are striking. Along the 83-mile Tualatin River, envisioned as a water trail in Metro’s 1992 Greenspaces Master Plan, protected land helps safeguard a river that supplies drinking water to about 400,000 people. Cooper Mountain near Beaverton was bought when it sat well outside the urban growth boundary; housing soon reached its edge, and waiting would have made it unaffordable. At North Multnomah Channel Marsh, a former dairy farm bought in 1997 became a 278-acre wetland after Metro removed three culverts and reconnected it to the water. More than a decade later, it supports juvenile salmon, northern red-legged frogs, bald eagles and beavers.

At Canemah Bluff, restoring an Oregon white oak savanna attracted at least a dozen bird species not previously recorded there. In the East Buttes, ancient lava domes more than 2 million years old hold some of the region’s largest connected wildlife habitat. More than a dozen natural areas along the Clackamas River help cool and clean a river that provides drinking water for 300,000 people.

How big is 20,000 acres? Metro offers comparisons: about 105 Hoyt Arboretums, 15,151 football fields, or almost four more Forest Parks.
stories.whyMatters: Three decades of voter-backed land protection keep Portland-area rivers clean and wild places close.

stories.title: A sandwich-shop owner swims the English Channel in 14 hours and raises $20,000 for clean water back home
stories.summary: Drew Nemetz, 44, of Port Chester, New York, swam from England to France in 14 hours and 16 minutes on Saturday, Oct. 3, becoming the year’s 92nd solo Channel swimmer. He trained in Long Island Sound and has raised more than $20,000 for the nonprofit Save the Sound.
stories.summaryLong:
Fourteen hours and 16 minutes after entering the water near Samphire Hoe on England’s southeast coast, Drew Nemetz stepped onto the beach at Cap Blanc-Nez, France, on Saturday afternoon, completing a solo swim across the English Channel, the Yonkers Times reports.

Nemetz, 44, of Port Chester, New York, became the 92nd swimmer to complete a solo crossing this year, according to the Channel Swimming Association. Fewer than 2,200 people have recorded successful solo crossings since 1875—less than one-third the number who have summited Mount Everest.

Nemetz, who owns Alpen Pantry, a sandwich shop in Old Greenwich, Connecticut, with his wife, Frannie Willsey, spent much of the year training. Many of his distance swims took place in Long Island Sound off Rye, so he paired his preparation with a campaign for clean water in the Sound, fundraising for Save the Sound, a regional environmental nonprofit. He has raised more than $20,000 so far.

“Accomplishing this swim was very meaningful for many reasons. I enjoyed the challenge, believe it or not, and this lovely area of the world. The conditions were difficult, but my crew and friends helped me get through it,” Nemetz said. “I am looking forward to getting back in my local waters of Long Island Sound to get ready for the next big swim.”

Save the Sound’s Peter Linderoth was part of his support team aboard the boat Masterpiece for the roughly 21-mile crossing. The crew handed him food and water, tallied his strokes per hour, monitored his health and safety—including helping him fend off a few aggressive jellyfish a couple of hours from the finish—and cheered him on. “It was amazing to watch Drew power through everything he encountered during a grueling crossing,” Linderoth said. “It was a once-in-a-lifetime privilege to be part of his support team on the water.”
stories.whyMatters: One swimmer’s 21-mile feat doubled as a fundraiser to keep his home waters clean.

stories.title: Portland Marathon draws a record of nearly 15,000 runners, and the winner was running his first marathon
stories.summary: The 54th Portland Marathon on Sunday, Oct. 4, had its biggest field yet—nearly 15,000 participants, organizers said. Connor Ford won overall in his first-ever marathon, and Portland local Margaret Glad led the women’s race.
stories.summaryLong:
Nearly 15,000 people took part in the 54th annual Portland Marathon on Sunday, the largest number to date, according to the organization, KPTV reports.

“With this being the city signature marathon, we understand the importance of community involvement and continue to put effort towards expanding our relationships and partnerships with local groups and organizations,” said Austri Biddinger, the marathon’s marketing lead. “Year-after-year we continue to see the runner’s experience grow and overall race demand increase.”

According to the Portland Marathon, men’s champion and overall first-place finisher Connor Ford completed his first marathon ever, in 2:27:17, followed by Jake Stout and Zach Steele. Portland local Margaret Glad led the women’s race in 2:52:42, followed by Jenna Schwartz and Maria Conti. JL Odom won the gender expansive division in 3:13:45, followed by Georgie Okell and Brook Lindsey.

The race is a Boston Marathon qualifier and drew runners from across the city, state and country—many running with a purpose. “It’s my first marathon so just happy to make it to the finish line,” said Benjamin Bazzel of Tigard. Laila Corzo of McHenry, Illinois, said she was hospitalized a few years ago and lost her ability to walk: “Now, I just run marathons for fun and I just do it for the people that can’t.”

Denise Polacek and her daughter Rebecca, both from Oregon, ran side by side for healing after a loss in their family. “It wasn’t so hard that you can’t do it,” Polacek said. “I’m 64. If I did it, they can do it.” Her daughter added, “It builds a lot of self-confidence to know that you can do this, even with minimal prep.”

The event, presented by Nike Running, also included a half marathon, 10K and Kids Run.
stories.summaryLongNote: Based on a short local TV report; results as stated by the organizers.
stories.whyMatters: Thousands of first-timers and comeback runners finished 26.2 miles together in Portland.

stories.title: Students build a voice-guided braille tutor in 24 hours and win a HackMIT challenge
stories.summary: Dakota State juniors Smaran Pokharel and Tenzing Gurung teamed with MIT freshmen Reagan Spurlock and Sage Peterson to build Braillie, a phone-based tutor that helps blind and low-vision learners practice reading braille. It won Deepgram’s “Build Something Worth Talking To” challenge.
stories.summaryLong:
With one hour left before the HackMIT deadline, the finger-tracking system at the heart of Braillie stopped working. Dakota State University juniors Smaran Pokharel and Tenzing Gurung scrambled to repair it, then demonstrated all three learning modes to judges—and won Deepgram’s “Build Something Worth Talking To” challenge, DSU’s Trojan Times reports.

Braillie is a voice-guided tutor designed to help blind and low-vision learners practice reading braille using a smartphone and a sheet of raised braille dots. “We started by researching the problem, which is how we decided to build something that teaches braille instead of just translating it,” Pokharel said. The pair teamed up with MIT freshmen Reagan Spurlock and Dorothy “Sage” Peterson, connecting through an online search for teammates.

A phone links to the system through a QR code, becoming camera, speaker and microphone. The learner holds the phone near their forehead with one hand while tracing the braille sheet with the other. A computer-vision system called BSeer detects the raised dots and identifies the letter under the learner’s finger, and a voice tutor named Braillo gives instructions and feedback. Read mode speaks the letter beneath the finger; Quiz mode asks learners to find a letter or word by touch; Learn mode offers guided lessons that revisit the letters each learner finds hardest. Spoken commands like “repeat,” “hint” and “stop” control the tutor.

The team split work by strengths: Pokharel built the vision system and tutoring functions, Gurung built the Deepgram voice system and led testing, Spurlock designed the website and presented to judges, and Peterson edited the demo video and made practice sheets by pressing raised dots into paper with the end of a paintbrush. Detecting tiny dots through a camera was hard—shadows, glare and angles interfered—and testing showed that holding the phone worked better than a stand, so they changed the design.

“To have Deepgram recognize Braillie meant a lot to us, because voice is at the very heart of what makes the project accessible,” Pokharel said. Judges encouraged the team to keep going, and they now plan to test the prototype with blind and low-vision learners and their teachers.
stories.whyMatters: Four students turned a weekend hackathon into a tool that could help blind learners read braille.

stories.title: Alexander Calder’s final sculpture is being made whole again on Capitol Hill after 12 years
stories.summary: Calder’s 51-foot “Mountains and Clouds” lost its hanging clouds in 2014 over structural fears. After 12 years and $12 million from two private donors, rebuilt carbon-fiber clouds are being rehung, and this time they are meant to rotate as Calder intended.
stories.summaryLong:
More than a decade after Alexander Calder’s final sculpture was disassembled and partly removed from the Hart Senate Office Building, the work is one step closer to returning in full, Smithsonian Magazine reports.

“Mountains and Clouds” is a 51-foot-tall installation of painted aluminum sheets and the famed sculptor’s only work that combines standing pieces—five triangular mountains—with his signature hanging mobile of four oval-ish clouds. It also represents his final act as an artist. In 1976 the design was chosen to fill the Senate building’s nine-story atrium; Calder spent his last day alive in Washington presenting a scaled model to officials and sizing up its future home. He died the next morning at 78. His estate approved the sculpture’s posthumous creation—the only time such permission was granted—and it was dedicated on May 5, 1987. The clouds alone weighed 4,300 pounds.

For roughly 30 years, the black landscape stood in striking contrast to the atrium’s white marble. But in 2014 the clouds were lowered over fears about their structural safety after a 2011 earthquake, and in 2016 they were removed completely. Critics said the sculpture lost its balance and meaning without them.

Now, 12 years and $12 million from two private donors later, the clouds have been rebuilt from brand-new sheets of a lighter carbon-fiber composite. Construction crews gathered inside the atrium in late September to begin reinstallation: hanging and balancing the clouds, then motorizing them so they gently rotate around the mountain peaks. That motion was part of Calder’s original plans, but difficulties during the first installation meant the clouds had stood still since 1992. Getting them to drift could take until sometime in November, officials speculate.

“We’re excited about the progress that has been made so far in this historic restoration and look forward to sharing more soon,” a Calder Foundation spokesperson told Roll Call.
stories.whyMatters: A master’s last artwork gets its missing half back—and may finally move as he designed it.

stories.title: Astoria’s new mural turns an old wall into a love letter to Oregon film, from “The Goonies” to “Twilight”
stories.summary: Local artist Jo Brown and her team unveiled a mural at 9th and Duane in Astoria celebrating more than 100 years of film in the town and across Oregon. It highlights 11 films and TV shows shot in the state, and a high-school junior helped paint it.
stories.summaryLong:
Astoria’s newest mural is now open to the public at 9th and Duane. Painted by local artist Jo Brown and her team of muralists, it celebrates more than 100 years of film in Astoria and across Oregon, The Astorian reports.

Community members, elected leaders, county officials and local radio station KRKZ—handing out “Shuffle Truffles”—came to the unveiling. “Now we have an eyesore that’s a photo op,” Brown said of the wall, formerly part of a dilapidated Darigold building. “We have a tall cement wall that tells our story.” She hopes it inspires more public art across the community, whether paintings, poems, sculptures or light installations.

The mural highlights 11 films and TV shows shot in Oregon: “Short Circuit,” “Twilight,” “The Shining,” “The Ring Two,” “Free Willy 2,” “Grimm,” “The Fisherman’s Bride,” “Wild,” “Benji the Hunted,” “Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles 3” and the ever-present crowd pleaser, “The Goonies.”

“This mural celebrates something that has become an important part of Clatsop County and Astoria’s story,” said County Commissioner Courtney Bangs, noting the history goes back to 1909, when “The Fisherman’s Bride” became the first film shot in Astoria and the first narrative film made in Oregon. She thanked the artists, county collaborators and neighbors who let their sidewalks be taken over during painting. Workers also replaced the cracked, aging sidewalk beside the wall so people can walk on level ground.

For Parker Pasco, an Astoria High School junior who helped paint it, the unveiling was a dream come true. “I’ve always wanted to be a part of a big community project like this and I’m so happy we were able to pull it off,” he said.

Brown hopes the newly formed Astoria Arts and Culture Commission, which begins meeting in 2027, will help bring more young artists into the community. “Let’s make these things happen and make Astoria pretty and inviting.”
stories.whyMatters: A neglected wall became a free, joyful public artwork that a teenager helped create.

stories.title: Coquille Tribe’s first salmon releases start coming home to an Oregon coast river
stories.summary: After the Coquille River’s Chinook run nearly vanished, the Coquille Indian Tribe and Oregon’s wildlife agency began co-managing a recovery: removing invasive bass and raising young salmon. Fish from the tribe’s first releases are now beginning to return.
stories.summaryLong:
At the Ko-Kwel Salmon Celebration on Oregon’s South Coast, tribal elder William Murphy has helped tend the charcoal pit for 19 years, sharing Coquille Indian culture through traditional canoes, the Miluk language, crafts, songs and acorn mush. One thing at the festival wasn’t local: the roughly half a ton of salmon it needs had to be bought from tribes on the Columbia River, because the Coquille River’s own run can’t yet provide it.

Starting around 2018, salmon returns crashed in many Oregon coastal rivers. Other basins recovered over the next couple of years, but the Coquille didn’t, said Ed Hughes, acting fish district biologist for the Oregon Department of Fish and Wildlife. That helped biologists connect the decline to invasive smallmouth bass, which prey on young salmon, alongside warmer water, low flows and changing ocean conditions.

The state brought its concerns to the tribal council. In 2022 the tribe and ODFW formalized a co-management agreement covering fish and wildlife across five southwest Oregon counties, and developed a conservation hatchery program to rebuild the Coquille’s wild fall Chinook. Their work has included removing invasive bass, improving collection of adult salmon for breeding and expanding hatchery efforts.

At Ferry Creek in Bandon, tribal fisheries workers stretch seine nets to guide hundreds of finger-sized smolts downstream. The fish are spawned at Bandon Hatchery, raised at Cole Rivers Hatchery and brought back to the creek to acclimate. “They get the scent of the river, and then they’re ready to go out to the ocean,” said fisheries technician Jesse Rodriguez. “We’re just trying to basically jump-start this whole population of salmon.”

Now there are signs of progress. Tribal chair Brenda Meade said fish from the tribe’s earlier releases are beginning to return: “This year is so important because that four-year rotation of the smolt that we were a part of releasing for the first time are now the fish that are coming back into the river.” The run is not yet recovered, but for Meade the work shows the value of Indigenous stewardship. “I couldn’t live in a world that there were no salmon in the Coquille River,” she said.
stories.whyMatters: Tribal and state co-management is giving a near-lost salmon run a real second chance.

stories.title: Webb’s “cosmic house of mirrors” shows galaxies stretched, bent and copied by a giant cluster’s gravity
stories.summary: The James Webb Space Telescope’s new Picture of the Month shows galaxy cluster MACS J0454.1-0300 bending light from far more distant galaxies into arcs and multiple images. Compared with Hubble’s 2014 view, it reveals hundreds of galaxies that were there all along.
stories.summaryLong:
The NASA/ESA/CSA James Webb Space Telescope’s Picture of the Month, released Sept. 29, features galaxies that look warped and multiplied as if they had stepped into a house of mirrors. The brilliant golden galaxies belong to a cluster called MACS J0454.1-0300, in the constellation Orion. We see it as it was when the universe was about 8 billion years old. The orange galaxies crowded to one side aren’t part of the cluster at all—they are much farther away.

The real stars of the image are those warped, stretched galaxies, “like a painting that has been smeared by a giant hand.” They are the result of gravitational lensing: the cluster’s enormous mass bends and magnifies light from objects behind it, letting astronomers see galaxies, star clusters and even individual stars too far away to observe normally. Look closely, ESA says, and even small reddish galaxies at the very edge of the frame are bent into tiny arcs.

Lensing can also make us see double—or quadruple. Seeing four or more images of one galaxy is rare, appearing in only 10–20% of galaxy clusters. Researchers spotted it twice in this cluster, the first time the phenomenon has been seen more than once in the same cluster. The lensed areas show a group of galaxies from 2 billion years after the Big Bang, apparently merging in a huge burst of star formation, and a single galaxy from just 800 million years after the Big Bang. Some bright knots as small as 5 light-years across appear magnified more than 300 times.

Hubble imaged the same cluster in 2014, and comparing the two is dramatic: Webb reveals hundreds of galaxies missing from the earlier picture, because it is far more sensitive to their redder light. The data come from two observing programs, one hunting for hugely magnified single stars from the universe’s first billion years and another surveying many galaxy clusters to study early star formation.
stories.whyMatters: A natural cosmic magnifying glass lets us see galaxies from the universe’s childhood.

stories.title: A wild stretch of Oregon coast near Yachats is returning to the Siletz Tribe after more than 170 years
stories.summary: Rocky Shores, a 6.82-acre parcel south of Yachats, is being returned to the Confederated Tribes of Siletz Indians with help from the McKenzie River Trust and conservation groups. The tribe plans to protect its stream, ferns and coastal plants rather than open it to the public.
stories.summaryLong:
In 1855, the Confederated Tribes of Siletz Indians ceded much of their ancestral land as the U.S. ratified treaties across Oregon. Now a small but treasured piece of it is coming back. Rocky Shores, a 6.82-acre area south of Yachats at an undisclosed location, fell into private ownership after colonization; with help from the McKenzie River Trust and conservation nonprofits including View the Future and The Nature Conservancy, it will soon return to the tribe’s stewardship, KLCC reports.

“This was part of our ancestral territories, and it was also part of the coast reservation,” said CTSI Natural Resources Director Angela Sondenaa, noting the treaty reservation once included 100 miles of the central Oregon coast. She described Rocky Shores as pristine and biodiverse: “There is a freshwater stream that runs through it. It’s rich in ferns and mosses and mushrooms. Abundant salal, other coastal species that are so critically important to us and our efforts to restore kelp and sea otters to our territory.”

Councilmember Robert Kentta shared a local legend that Oregon’s largest-ever Dungeness crab was caught there decades ago, but said the tribe will survey the property’s sensitive species and features, and warned its cliff-like terrain is dangerous.

After negotiations and appraisals, the land was bought for $120,000, with Joanne Kittel’s group View the Future contributing $55,000. “We knew it had to be safe,” Kittel said. “We knew it had to be protected and we knew it had to go to the tribes.” The transfer was expected within days, with the McKenzie River Trust acting as intermediary and using flexible funding so the title carries no restrictions. “The tribe really can make the decisions for how they want to manage this land in perpetuity,” said the trust’s conservation director, Eli Tome.

Executive director Joe Moll called the growing collaboration between land trusts and tribal nations “really, really satisfying… It’s joyful work and we’ll continue with it.” The tribe won’t open Rocky Shores to the public, to protect the ecosystem, though it may host invited events. Council member Alfred “Buddy” Lane IV said Siletz elders once sustained themselves on mussels from these rocks, adding, “I am excited for our people to reestablish our connection to this place.”
stories.whyMatters: A pristine coastal parcel returns to the people who cared for it first, protected for good.

stories.title: Four young California condors take flight from Arizona’s Vermilion Cliffs at the 30th annual release
stories.summary: On Sept. 26, the Peregrine Fund released four captive-born California condors above a 4,000-foot cliff north of the Grand Canyon, joining a flock of 92 in Arizona and Utah. Thirty years ago only 29 condors lived in the wild; as of last year there were 392.
stories.summaryLong:
Above a 4,000-foot cliff near Arizona’s border with Utah, avian biologists opened a cage door and waited. Twenty long minutes later, Condor 1365—the only male of the group—shot out and soared west toward the Kaibab Plateau on a thermal, The Arizona Republic reports. It was the first flight of the 30th annual California condor release near the Vermilion Cliffs, watched by more than a hundred bird enthusiasts in camp chairs below.

Since 1997, the Peregrine Fund, a nonprofit for birds of prey, has worked to bring California condors back from near extinction by releasing captive-born birds into their native range. On Sept. 26, four new condors joined a flock of 92 in Arizona and Utah. “We have historic evidence of condors in the Grand Canyon,” said biologist Emma Heydenberk. “They’ve always been a part of this ecosystem.” With nine-foot wingspans, they are the largest birds by wingspan in North America.

All four hatched at a captive breeding facility in Boise last spring and were driven south by biologist Julia Schmidt, who spent a month preparing them. Each has a distinct personality. “I have a feeling this particular group of birds is going to do very well,” she said. The team tracks the birds by radio and GPS every morning, feeds them and removes dangerous roadkill.

Lead poisoning from spent ammunition remains the leading cause of condor deaths, and Arizona Game and Fish has worked with hunters since 2005, offering lead-free ammunition. Participation has grown from about half of hunters in the condor range to 85%.

There is real progress. The first wild fledge happened in 2003 in Grand Canyon National Park, and since then 74 condors have hatched in the wild between Arizona and Utah. Thirty years ago, only 29 condors lived in the wild; as of last year, 392 did—though the species is still critically endangered. “This is a very old species,” said program director Tim Hauck. “They survived the last ice age. Condors are resilient.” From the moment the doors opened, it took just 49 minutes for all four birds to take to the skies.
stories.whyMatters: Thirty years of patient work has grown the wild condor population from 29 to 392.

stories.title: Meet the 20 new MacArthur Fellows, from a sea-ice scientist to a saxophonist who cooks onstage
stories.summary: The MacArthur Foundation named 20 new fellows, each receiving a no-strings-attached $800,000 grant. This year’s class spans climate scientists, chemists, historians, poets, visual artists and a 29-year-old jazz saxophonist.
stories.summaryLong:
The MacArthur Foundation has named 20 new recipients of its no-strings-attached, $800,000 fellowship grants, popularly known as “genius grants,” NPR reports via GPB. As usual, the winners, selected through the foundation’s network of scouts, come from a wide range of disciplines.

Several are working on climate and food. Kaiyu Guan, a climate scientist at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, combines satellite data and machine learning to boost food productivity while reducing environmental impacts, including digital platforms that simulate how crops might respond to future weather, water availability and land management. Marika Holland, at the National Center for Atmospheric Research in Boulder, Colorado, studies how polar sea ice interacts with global climate. Holly Jean Buck, a University at Buffalo sociologist, examines the ethics of climate policy and argues carbon removal should serve local communities.

Others are opening new paths in health and chemistry. UC San Diego engineer Liangfang Zhang pioneered cloaking synthetic nanoparticles in natural cell membranes so they can deliver drugs and neutralize toxins without being rejected by the immune system. Stanford organic chemist Song Lin has shown how simple electrical currents—even from a couple of AA batteries—can replace expensive, toxic heavy metals to build complex molecules for medicine. University of Chicago physicist Vincenzo Vitelli uses topology to model how forces move through living tissue, informing understanding of growth and wound healing.

The arts are well represented. Christine Sun Kim, a Berlin-based artist born deaf, makes large charcoal drawings that combine musical notation with American Sign Language grammar to make ASL’s nuances visible to non-signers. Texas painter Vincent Valdez depicts everyday working-class people, particularly from Chicano communities. Santa Fe poet Layli Long Soldier, novelist Bryan Washington and novelist Maaza Mengiste are also honored, along with Zürich-based choreographer Trajal Harrell.

The youngest fellow is 29-year-old New York saxophonist and composer Immanuel Wilkins, who turns concert venues into multisensory spaces—once performing alongside a chef cooking onstage, with chopping, boiling and frying folded into the music. The oldest, at 69, is Flagstaff, Arizona, visual artist Chip Thomas, whose 36 years as a primary care physician on the Navajo Nation inform his work. Historians, economists, a philosopher and a forensic anthropologist round out the class.
stories.whyMatters: Twenty creative people get five years of freedom to pursue work that helps us see and live better.

stories.title: MIT engineers build a paper-thin robot that swims a maze powered by a single layer of muscle cells
stories.summary: An MIT team led by Ritu Raman made a gum-stick-sized gel robot whose two fins are coated with light-sensitive muscle cells. Flashing light on either fin steers it, and it swam and swiveled through a simple watery maze.
stories.summaryLong:
Swimming takes a lot of muscle, but MIT engineers have found that even a single layer of muscle cells can power through water if designed right. In a paper in Advanced Functional Materials, the team presents a thin, muscle-powered swimming robot whose gel “skeleton” is about the length and width of a stick of gum. Each half forms a fin covered with a layer of live muscle cells thinner than a strand of hair, genetically engineered to twitch in response to light.

Shining light on one fin makes it flap with enough force to pull the robot through water; flashing either fin at different intervals controls direction and speed. The bot swam and swiveled through a simple maze in a petri dish. At its fastest it covers about four body lengths per minute—a snail’s pace next to Olympic swimmers, but on par with the leisurely cow shark. “The robot’s quite strong, given its size,” said Ritu Raman, associate professor of mechanical engineering. MIT says it is the first very thin, two-dimensional, muscle-powered robot capable of locomotion.

Most biohybrid robots use bulky 3D chunks of lab-grown muscle requiring millions of cells. Thinner designs could be cheaper and more efficient. The key was optimizing the skeleton. The team swapped ultrasoft fibrin for a stiffer gel called gelatin methacrylate, stamped it with square-bottomed grooves that helped cells align and fuse into strong fibers, settled on a half-millimeter-thin film, and even “exercised” the muscles with a light-flashing training routine.

“You can think of the robot as having two independent muscles,” Raman said. “If we shine a light on just one, only that muscle moves.” Next the team wants to improve the body design for faster swimming. Raman believes muscle-powered robots could one day explore environments too fragile for conventional hardware, “because living tissue is soft, responsive to its surroundings, and can heal itself,” and imagines uses like environmental monitoring in water. First author is Maheera Bawa.
stories.whyMatters: Soft, living robots could someday gently explore places too delicate for metal machines.

stories.title: OHSU becomes first in Oregon to use vagus-nerve implants to help stroke and arthritis patients heal
stories.summary: Neurosurgeons at Oregon Health & Science University are the first in Oregon to implant small FDA-approved devices on the vagus nerve to promote healing. One device helps the brain rewire after stroke; the other aims to calm the inflammation behind rheumatoid arthritis.
stories.summaryLong:
Neurosurgeons at Oregon Health & Science University have reached a medical milestone: they are the first in Oregon to implant small devices on the vagus nerve to promote healing. The vagus nerve is the longest cranial nerve in the body, and the FDA-approved devices send small, precisely targeted electrical impulses along it to the brainstem. Patients barely feel the signal.

“This will be life-altering treatment for a lot of patients,” said Ahmed Raslan, M.D., chair of neurological surgery in the OHSU School of Medicine. “It opens up a new era in bioelectronic medicine.”

For stroke rehabilitation, a thumb-size device is implanted under the skin of the chest with a wire to the left vagus nerve, in an outpatient procedure—people go home the same day. “By stimulating the vagus nerve, you stimulate new synapse connections in the brain,” said neurosurgeon Adam Lipson, M.D., who performed OHSU’s first two stroke cases on Sept. 4. “You’re assisting the brain to reorganize and supplant the pathways that were damaged by the stroke.”

Both of those first patients hope to get back to horses. Lauren Vogel, 47, of La Center, Washington, is walking again after a 2023 stroke but still lacks function in the fingers of her left hand—a major problem since she is left-handed. She envisions returning to work as a horse trainer. “Nothing’s guaranteed, but we’re hopeful and I’ll definitely put the work in,” she said. Stacey Leah Melvin, 58, of Eagle Point in Southern Oregon, wants to be able to help her 18-year-old son, including handing him a brush or holding his horses when he shows them.

For rheumatoid arthritis, OHSU is the first in the Pacific Northwest to offer the treatment. Raslan implanted a vitamin-sized wireless device in the neck, connected to the left vagus nerve. Brooke Braun, 48, of Wilsonville, one of the first patients on Aug. 25, has had arthritis since age 23 and was glad to receive the treatment close to home; it is too early to know whether it helps.

Rheumatologist Cong-Qiu Chu, M.D., Ph.D., explained that the vagus nerve normally senses an immune overreaction and signals the immune system to calm down. Stimulating it “may benefit patients who aren’t responsive to available medications,” he said, describing the device as a complementary therapy.
stories.whyMatters: Oregon patients can now get bioelectronic therapies for stroke recovery and arthritis close to home.

stories.title: An orphaned gorilla returned to the wild has become a mother, a first for her species
stories.summary: Lulingu, rescued as an 18-month-old from the illegal wildlife trade, was one of four eastern lowland gorillas rewilded into Virunga National Park in late 2024. She has given birth to an infant fathered by a wild silverback, and both are healthy.
stories.summaryLong:
One of the first eastern lowland gorillas ever successfully returned to the wild gave birth on May 21 in Virunga National Park in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Good News Network reports—a historic first for the species’ conservation.

The mother, Lulingu, was one of four female gorillas moved at the end of 2024 from the GRACE sanctuary in North Kivu province to Virunga. Her baby was fathered by a wild silverback living on Mount Tshiaberimu, a sign she has integrated into the wild population. Rescuers recovered Lulingu when she was just 18 months old after she was taken from her family and sold into the illegal wildlife trade; she was the youngest orphan ever brought to GRACE, the only sanctuary in the world for rescued eastern lowland gorillas. There, a gorilla named Pinga became her surrogate mother.

The release of the four females—Lulingu, Mapendo, Ndjingala and Isangi—capped a more-than-five-year rewilding process led by GRACE, Virunga National Park and local communities, with support from Gorilla Doctors and Re:wild. The birth also advances a central goal: a genetic boost for the small, isolated gorilla population on Tshiaberimu.

Monitors have tracked the group closely, even collecting urine from leaves and using human pregnancy tests to detect pregnancy hormones. “None of the 4 females have required veterinary treatment for illness or injury since being rewilded,” said Gorilla Doctors veterinarian Dr. Cedric Kibengo. “Both mother and infant are healthy and doing well.” Ranger Benoit Ishaba said the team has seen Lulingu “nursing, cradling, and playing with the baby.”

“This is a milestone for the gorillas,” said Katie Fawcett of GRACE Gorillas, adding the team is cautiously optimistic. At least one other rewilded female may also be pregnant. “Each healthy infant represents more than an addition to the population—it is a sign of resilience, recovery, and what is possible,” said Re:wild’s Mary Brown.
stories.whyMatters: A rescued orphan is now raising the next generation of a critically endangered gorilla.

pool.title: Crew-13 reaches the space station in 7 hours 55 minutes, the fastest trip ever for a U.S. spacecraft
pool.summary: SpaceX’s Crew-13 mission for NASA docked with the International Space Station on Oct. 1, just 7 hours and 55 minutes after launching from Florida. NASA officials said it was the fastest any American spacecraft has ever reached the orbiting lab.
pool.summaryLong:
SpaceX’s Crew-13 mission for NASA arrived at the International Space Station on Thursday, Oct. 1, at 7:05 p.m. EDT—7 hours and 55 minutes after it launched from Florida’s Space Coast. NASA officials said that is the fastest any American spacecraft has ever reached the orbiting lab.

The previous record for a U.S. vehicle was 12 hours and 33 minutes, set in November 2024 by SpaceX’s Dragon cargo capsule on the robotic CRS-31 resupply flight. The fastest astronauts had made the trip in a U.S. vehicle was 14 hours and 43 minutes, achieved by the Crew-11 mission in August 2025.

“We got lucky this time,” Julianna Scheiman, SpaceX’s director of NASA science and Dragon programs, said at the post-launch press conference. “The space station was in an opportune spot in space, and the orbital mechanics, the physics of it all, worked out for it to be the shortest launch-to-docking time we’ve had to date,” she said, adding that “this is close to the fastest it could be.”

Crew-13 did not set the overall speed record to the station—a Russian Soyuz carrying three astronauts once reached the lab just 3 hours and 3 minutes after liftoff. Space.com notes the Soyuz isn’t faster or more powerful than a Dragon; the difference comes mainly from mission controllers choosing more aggressive “fast-track” trajectories.

Crew-13 delivered four astronauts: NASA’s Jessica Watkins and Luke Delaney, Joshua Kutryk of the Canadian Space Agency and Sergey Teteryatnikov of Roscosmos. The quartet will live and work in space for the next six months, relieving the four members of Crew-12—NASA astronauts Jessica Meir and Jack Hathaway, ESA’s Sophie Adenot and cosmonaut Andrey Fedyaev—who launched in mid-February and are preparing to return to Earth in their Crew Dragon capsule.
pool.whyMatters: A smooth, record-quick handoff keeps four new crew members working on the station for six months.

pool.title: Greater Portland’s Metro reaches 20,000 acres of protected parks and natural areas
pool.summary: Metro’s portfolio of parks, natural areas, trails and historic cemeteries has hit 20,000 acres, a milestone more than three decades in the making. Voters funded it through three parks-and-nature bonds and a levy, and the land protects salmon habitat and drinking water for hundreds of thousands of people.
pool.summaryLong:
This year, Metro, greater Portland’s regional government, is celebrating a major conservation milestone: its portfolio of green spaces has reached 20,000 acres. It started with a few thousand acres transferred from Portland and Multnomah County in the early 1990s and has grown into a network of parks, natural areas, regional trails and historic cemeteries meant to protect the region’s water quality and natural beauty.

Metro didn’t do it alone. Voters across the region passed three parks and nature bonds that funded land purchases and passed and renewed a levy that supports ongoing care. Other agencies, community organizations and tribal governments helped set priorities, and property owners chose to sell or donate land for nature.

The stories behind the map are striking. Along the 83-mile Tualatin River, envisioned as a water trail in Metro’s 1992 Greenspaces Master Plan, protected land helps safeguard a river that supplies drinking water to about 400,000 people. Cooper Mountain near Beaverton was bought when it sat well outside the urban growth boundary; housing soon reached its edge, and waiting would have made it unaffordable. At North Multnomah Channel Marsh, a former dairy farm bought in 1997 became a 278-acre wetland after Metro removed three culverts and reconnected it to the water. More than a decade later, it supports juvenile salmon, northern red-legged frogs, bald eagles and beavers.

At Canemah Bluff, restoring an Oregon white oak savanna attracted at least a dozen bird species not previously recorded there. In the East Buttes, ancient lava domes more than 2 million years old hold some of the region’s largest connected wildlife habitat. More than a dozen natural areas along the Clackamas River help cool and clean a river that provides drinking water for 300,000 people.

How big is 20,000 acres? Metro offers comparisons: about 105 Hoyt Arboretums, 15,151 football fields, or almost four more Forest Parks.
pool.whyMatters: Three decades of voter-backed land protection keep Portland-area rivers clean and wild places close.

pool.title: A sandwich-shop owner swims the English Channel in 14 hours and raises $20,000 for clean water back home
pool.summary: Drew Nemetz, 44, of Port Chester, New York, swam from England to France in 14 hours and 16 minutes on Saturday, Oct. 3, becoming the year’s 92nd solo Channel swimmer. He trained in Long Island Sound and has raised more than $20,000 for the nonprofit Save the Sound.
pool.summaryLong:
Fourteen hours and 16 minutes after entering the water near Samphire Hoe on England’s southeast coast, Drew Nemetz stepped onto the beach at Cap Blanc-Nez, France, on Saturday afternoon, completing a solo swim across the English Channel, the Yonkers Times reports.

Nemetz, 44, of Port Chester, New York, became the 92nd swimmer to complete a solo crossing this year, according to the Channel Swimming Association. Fewer than 2,200 people have recorded successful solo crossings since 1875—less than one-third the number who have summited Mount Everest.

Nemetz, who owns Alpen Pantry, a sandwich shop in Old Greenwich, Connecticut, with his wife, Frannie Willsey, spent much of the year training. Many of his distance swims took place in Long Island Sound off Rye, so he paired his preparation with a campaign for clean water in the Sound, fundraising for Save the Sound, a regional environmental nonprofit. He has raised more than $20,000 so far.

“Accomplishing this swim was very meaningful for many reasons. I enjoyed the challenge, believe it or not, and this lovely area of the world. The conditions were difficult, but my crew and friends helped me get through it,” Nemetz said. “I am looking forward to getting back in my local waters of Long Island Sound to get ready for the next big swim.”

Save the Sound’s Peter Linderoth was part of his support team aboard the boat Masterpiece for the roughly 21-mile crossing. The crew handed him food and water, tallied his strokes per hour, monitored his health and safety—including helping him fend off a few aggressive jellyfish a couple of hours from the finish—and cheered him on. “It was amazing to watch Drew power through everything he encountered during a grueling crossing,” Linderoth said. “It was a once-in-a-lifetime privilege to be part of his support team on the water.”
pool.whyMatters: One swimmer’s 21-mile feat doubled as a fundraiser to keep his home waters clean.

pool.title: Portland Marathon draws a record of nearly 15,000 runners, and the winner was running his first marathon
pool.summary: The 54th Portland Marathon on Sunday, Oct. 4, had its biggest field yet—nearly 15,000 participants, organizers said. Connor Ford won overall in his first-ever marathon, and Portland local Margaret Glad led the women’s race.
pool.summaryLong:
Nearly 15,000 people took part in the 54th annual Portland Marathon on Sunday, the largest number to date, according to the organization, KPTV reports.

“With this being the city signature marathon, we understand the importance of community involvement and continue to put effort towards expanding our relationships and partnerships with local groups and organizations,” said Austri Biddinger, the marathon’s marketing lead. “Year-after-year we continue to see the runner’s experience grow and overall race demand increase.”

According to the Portland Marathon, men’s champion and overall first-place finisher Connor Ford completed his first marathon ever, in 2:27:17, followed by Jake Stout and Zach Steele. Portland local Margaret Glad led the women’s race in 2:52:42, followed by Jenna Schwartz and Maria Conti. JL Odom won the gender expansive division in 3:13:45, followed by Georgie Okell and Brook Lindsey.

The race is a Boston Marathon qualifier and drew runners from across the city, state and country—many running with a purpose. “It’s my first marathon so just happy to make it to the finish line,” said Benjamin Bazzel of Tigard. Laila Corzo of McHenry, Illinois, said she was hospitalized a few years ago and lost her ability to walk: “Now, I just run marathons for fun and I just do it for the people that can’t.”

Denise Polacek and her daughter Rebecca, both from Oregon, ran side by side for healing after a loss in their family. “It wasn’t so hard that you can’t do it,” Polacek said. “I’m 64. If I did it, they can do it.” Her daughter added, “It builds a lot of self-confidence to know that you can do this, even with minimal prep.”

The event, presented by Nike Running, also included a half marathon, 10K and Kids Run.
pool.summaryLongNote: Based on a short local TV report; results as stated by the organizers.
pool.whyMatters: Thousands of first-timers and comeback runners finished 26.2 miles together in Portland.

pool.title: Students build a voice-guided braille tutor in 24 hours and win a HackMIT challenge
pool.summary: Dakota State juniors Smaran Pokharel and Tenzing Gurung teamed with MIT freshmen Reagan Spurlock and Sage Peterson to build Braillie, a phone-based tutor that helps blind and low-vision learners practice reading braille. It won Deepgram’s “Build Something Worth Talking To” challenge.
pool.summaryLong:
With one hour left before the HackMIT deadline, the finger-tracking system at the heart of Braillie stopped working. Dakota State University juniors Smaran Pokharel and Tenzing Gurung scrambled to repair it, then demonstrated all three learning modes to judges—and won Deepgram’s “Build Something Worth Talking To” challenge, DSU’s Trojan Times reports.

Braillie is a voice-guided tutor designed to help blind and low-vision learners practice reading braille using a smartphone and a sheet of raised braille dots. “We started by researching the problem, which is how we decided to build something that teaches braille instead of just translating it,” Pokharel said. The pair teamed up with MIT freshmen Reagan Spurlock and Dorothy “Sage” Peterson, connecting through an online search for teammates.

A phone links to the system through a QR code, becoming camera, speaker and microphone. The learner holds the phone near their forehead with one hand while tracing the braille sheet with the other. A computer-vision system called BSeer detects the raised dots and identifies the letter under the learner’s finger, and a voice tutor named Braillo gives instructions and feedback. Read mode speaks the letter beneath the finger; Quiz mode asks learners to find a letter or word by touch; Learn mode offers guided lessons that revisit the letters each learner finds hardest. Spoken commands like “repeat,” “hint” and “stop” control the tutor.

The team split work by strengths: Pokharel built the vision system and tutoring functions, Gurung built the Deepgram voice system and led testing, Spurlock designed the website and presented to judges, and Peterson edited the demo video and made practice sheets by pressing raised dots into paper with the end of a paintbrush. Detecting tiny dots through a camera was hard—shadows, glare and angles interfered—and testing showed that holding the phone worked better than a stand, so they changed the design.

“To have Deepgram recognize Braillie meant a lot to us, because voice is at the very heart of what makes the project accessible,” Pokharel said. Judges encouraged the team to keep going, and they now plan to test the prototype with blind and low-vision learners and their teachers.
pool.whyMatters: Four students turned a weekend hackathon into a tool that could help blind learners read braille.

pool.title: Alexander Calder’s final sculpture is being made whole again on Capitol Hill after 12 years
pool.summary: Calder’s 51-foot “Mountains and Clouds” lost its hanging clouds in 2014 over structural fears. After 12 years and $12 million from two private donors, rebuilt carbon-fiber clouds are being rehung, and this time they are meant to rotate as Calder intended.
pool.summaryLong:
More than a decade after Alexander Calder’s final sculpture was disassembled and partly removed from the Hart Senate Office Building, the work is one step closer to returning in full, Smithsonian Magazine reports.

“Mountains and Clouds” is a 51-foot-tall installation of painted aluminum sheets and the famed sculptor’s only work that combines standing pieces—five triangular mountains—with his signature hanging mobile of four oval-ish clouds. It also represents his final act as an artist. In 1976 the design was chosen to fill the Senate building’s nine-story atrium; Calder spent his last day alive in Washington presenting a scaled model to officials and sizing up its future home. He died the next morning at 78. His estate approved the sculpture’s posthumous creation—the only time such permission was granted—and it was dedicated on May 5, 1987. The clouds alone weighed 4,300 pounds.

For roughly 30 years, the black landscape stood in striking contrast to the atrium’s white marble. But in 2014 the clouds were lowered over fears about their structural safety after a 2011 earthquake, and in 2016 they were removed completely. Critics said the sculpture lost its balance and meaning without them.

Now, 12 years and $12 million from two private donors later, the clouds have been rebuilt from brand-new sheets of a lighter carbon-fiber composite. Construction crews gathered inside the atrium in late September to begin reinstallation: hanging and balancing the clouds, then motorizing them so they gently rotate around the mountain peaks. That motion was part of Calder’s original plans, but difficulties during the first installation meant the clouds had stood still since 1992. Getting them to drift could take until sometime in November, officials speculate.

“We’re excited about the progress that has been made so far in this historic restoration and look forward to sharing more soon,” a Calder Foundation spokesperson told Roll Call.
pool.whyMatters: A master’s last artwork gets its missing half back—and may finally move as he designed it.

pool.title: Astoria’s new mural turns an old wall into a love letter to Oregon film, from “The Goonies” to “Twilight”
pool.summary: Local artist Jo Brown and her team unveiled a mural at 9th and Duane in Astoria celebrating more than 100 years of film in the town and across Oregon. It highlights 11 films and TV shows shot in the state, and a high-school junior helped paint it.
pool.summaryLong:
Astoria’s newest mural is now open to the public at 9th and Duane. Painted by local artist Jo Brown and her team of muralists, it celebrates more than 100 years of film in Astoria and across Oregon, The Astorian reports.

Community members, elected leaders, county officials and local radio station KRKZ—handing out “Shuffle Truffles”—came to the unveiling. “Now we have an eyesore that’s a photo op,” Brown said of the wall, formerly part of a dilapidated Darigold building. “We have a tall cement wall that tells our story.” She hopes it inspires more public art across the community, whether paintings, poems, sculptures or light installations.

The mural highlights 11 films and TV shows shot in Oregon: “Short Circuit,” “Twilight,” “The Shining,” “The Ring Two,” “Free Willy 2,” “Grimm,” “The Fisherman’s Bride,” “Wild,” “Benji the Hunted,” “Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles 3” and the ever-present crowd pleaser, “The Goonies.”

“This mural celebrates something that has become an important part of Clatsop County and Astoria’s story,” said County Commissioner Courtney Bangs, noting the history goes back to 1909, when “The Fisherman’s Bride” became the first film shot in Astoria and the first narrative film made in Oregon. She thanked the artists, county collaborators and neighbors who let their sidewalks be taken over during painting. Workers also replaced the cracked, aging sidewalk beside the wall so people can walk on level ground.

For Parker Pasco, an Astoria High School junior who helped paint it, the unveiling was a dream come true. “I’ve always wanted to be a part of a big community project like this and I’m so happy we were able to pull it off,” he said.

Brown hopes the newly formed Astoria Arts and Culture Commission, which begins meeting in 2027, will help bring more young artists into the community. “Let’s make these things happen and make Astoria pretty and inviting.”
pool.whyMatters: A neglected wall became a free, joyful public artwork that a teenager helped create.

pool.title: Coquille Tribe’s first salmon releases start coming home to an Oregon coast river
pool.summary: After the Coquille River’s Chinook run nearly vanished, the Coquille Indian Tribe and Oregon’s wildlife agency began co-managing a recovery: removing invasive bass and raising young salmon. Fish from the tribe’s first releases are now beginning to return.
pool.summaryLong:
At the Ko-Kwel Salmon Celebration on Oregon’s South Coast, tribal elder William Murphy has helped tend the charcoal pit for 19 years, sharing Coquille Indian culture through traditional canoes, the Miluk language, crafts, songs and acorn mush. One thing at the festival wasn’t local: the roughly half a ton of salmon it needs had to be bought from tribes on the Columbia River, because the Coquille River’s own run can’t yet provide it.

Starting around 2018, salmon returns crashed in many Oregon coastal rivers. Other basins recovered over the next couple of years, but the Coquille didn’t, said Ed Hughes, acting fish district biologist for the Oregon Department of Fish and Wildlife. That helped biologists connect the decline to invasive smallmouth bass, which prey on young salmon, alongside warmer water, low flows and changing ocean conditions.

The state brought its concerns to the tribal council. In 2022 the tribe and ODFW formalized a co-management agreement covering fish and wildlife across five southwest Oregon counties, and developed a conservation hatchery program to rebuild the Coquille’s wild fall Chinook. Their work has included removing invasive bass, improving collection of adult salmon for breeding and expanding hatchery efforts.

At Ferry Creek in Bandon, tribal fisheries workers stretch seine nets to guide hundreds of finger-sized smolts downstream. The fish are spawned at Bandon Hatchery, raised at Cole Rivers Hatchery and brought back to the creek to acclimate. “They get the scent of the river, and then they’re ready to go out to the ocean,” said fisheries technician Jesse Rodriguez. “We’re just trying to basically jump-start this whole population of salmon.”

Now there are signs of progress. Tribal chair Brenda Meade said fish from the tribe’s earlier releases are beginning to return: “This year is so important because that four-year rotation of the smolt that we were a part of releasing for the first time are now the fish that are coming back into the river.” The run is not yet recovered, but for Meade the work shows the value of Indigenous stewardship. “I couldn’t live in a world that there were no salmon in the Coquille River,” she said.
pool.whyMatters: Tribal and state co-management is giving a near-lost salmon run a real second chance.

pool.title: Webb’s “cosmic house of mirrors” shows galaxies stretched, bent and copied by a giant cluster’s gravity
pool.summary: The James Webb Space Telescope’s new Picture of the Month shows galaxy cluster MACS J0454.1-0300 bending light from far more distant galaxies into arcs and multiple images. Compared with Hubble’s 2014 view, it reveals hundreds of galaxies that were there all along.
pool.summaryLong:
The NASA/ESA/CSA James Webb Space Telescope’s Picture of the Month, released Sept. 29, features galaxies that look warped and multiplied as if they had stepped into a house of mirrors. The brilliant golden galaxies belong to a cluster called MACS J0454.1-0300, in the constellation Orion. We see it as it was when the universe was about 8 billion years old. The orange galaxies crowded to one side aren’t part of the cluster at all—they are much farther away.

The real stars of the image are those warped, stretched galaxies, “like a painting that has been smeared by a giant hand.” They are the result of gravitational lensing: the cluster’s enormous mass bends and magnifies light from objects behind it, letting astronomers see galaxies, star clusters and even individual stars too far away to observe normally. Look closely, ESA says, and even small reddish galaxies at the very edge of the frame are bent into tiny arcs.

Lensing can also make us see double—or quadruple. Seeing four or more images of one galaxy is rare, appearing in only 10–20% of galaxy clusters. Researchers spotted it twice in this cluster, the first time the phenomenon has been seen more than once in the same cluster. The lensed areas show a group of galaxies from 2 billion years after the Big Bang, apparently merging in a huge burst of star formation, and a single galaxy from just 800 million years after the Big Bang. Some bright knots as small as 5 light-years across appear magnified more than 300 times.

Hubble imaged the same cluster in 2014, and comparing the two is dramatic: Webb reveals hundreds of galaxies missing from the earlier picture, because it is far more sensitive to their redder light. The data come from two observing programs, one hunting for hugely magnified single stars from the universe’s first billion years and another surveying many galaxy clusters to study early star formation.
pool.whyMatters: A natural cosmic magnifying glass lets us see galaxies from the universe’s childhood.

pool.title: A wild stretch of Oregon coast near Yachats is returning to the Siletz Tribe after more than 170 years
pool.summary: Rocky Shores, a 6.82-acre parcel south of Yachats, is being returned to the Confederated Tribes of Siletz Indians with help from the McKenzie River Trust and conservation groups. The tribe plans to protect its stream, ferns and coastal plants rather than open it to the public.
pool.summaryLong:
In 1855, the Confederated Tribes of Siletz Indians ceded much of their ancestral land as the U.S. ratified treaties across Oregon. Now a small but treasured piece of it is coming back. Rocky Shores, a 6.82-acre area south of Yachats at an undisclosed location, fell into private ownership after colonization; with help from the McKenzie River Trust and conservation nonprofits including View the Future and The Nature Conservancy, it will soon return to the tribe’s stewardship, KLCC reports.

“This was part of our ancestral territories, and it was also part of the coast reservation,” said CTSI Natural Resources Director Angela Sondenaa, noting the treaty reservation once included 100 miles of the central Oregon coast. She described Rocky Shores as pristine and biodiverse: “There is a freshwater stream that runs through it. It’s rich in ferns and mosses and mushrooms. Abundant salal, other coastal species that are so critically important to us and our efforts to restore kelp and sea otters to our territory.”

Councilmember Robert Kentta shared a local legend that Oregon’s largest-ever Dungeness crab was caught there decades ago, but said the tribe will survey the property’s sensitive species and features, and warned its cliff-like terrain is dangerous.

After negotiations and appraisals, the land was bought for $120,000, with Joanne Kittel’s group View the Future contributing $55,000. “We knew it had to be safe,” Kittel said. “We knew it had to be protected and we knew it had to go to the tribes.” The transfer was expected within days, with the McKenzie River Trust acting as intermediary and using flexible funding so the title carries no restrictions. “The tribe really can make the decisions for how they want to manage this land in perpetuity,” said the trust’s conservation director, Eli Tome.

Executive director Joe Moll called the growing collaboration between land trusts and tribal nations “really, really satisfying… It’s joyful work and we’ll continue with it.” The tribe won’t open Rocky Shores to the public, to protect the ecosystem, though it may host invited events. Council member Alfred “Buddy” Lane IV said Siletz elders once sustained themselves on mussels from these rocks, adding, “I am excited for our people to reestablish our connection to this place.”
pool.whyMatters: A pristine coastal parcel returns to the people who cared for it first, protected for good.

pool.title: Four young California condors take flight from Arizona’s Vermilion Cliffs at the 30th annual release
pool.summary: On Sept. 26, the Peregrine Fund released four captive-born California condors above a 4,000-foot cliff north of the Grand Canyon, joining a flock of 92 in Arizona and Utah. Thirty years ago only 29 condors lived in the wild; as of last year there were 392.
pool.summaryLong:
Above a 4,000-foot cliff near Arizona’s border with Utah, avian biologists opened a cage door and waited. Twenty long minutes later, Condor 1365—the only male of the group—shot out and soared west toward the Kaibab Plateau on a thermal, The Arizona Republic reports. It was the first flight of the 30th annual California condor release near the Vermilion Cliffs, watched by more than a hundred bird enthusiasts in camp chairs below.

Since 1997, the Peregrine Fund, a nonprofit for birds of prey, has worked to bring California condors back from near extinction by releasing captive-born birds into their native range. On Sept. 26, four new condors joined a flock of 92 in Arizona and Utah. “We have historic evidence of condors in the Grand Canyon,” said biologist Emma Heydenberk. “They’ve always been a part of this ecosystem.” With nine-foot wingspans, they are the largest birds by wingspan in North America.

All four hatched at a captive breeding facility in Boise last spring and were driven south by biologist Julia Schmidt, who spent a month preparing them. Each has a distinct personality. “I have a feeling this particular group of birds is going to do very well,” she said. The team tracks the birds by radio and GPS every morning, feeds them and removes dangerous roadkill.

Lead poisoning from spent ammunition remains the leading cause of condor deaths, and Arizona Game and Fish has worked with hunters since 2005, offering lead-free ammunition. Participation has grown from about half of hunters in the condor range to 85%.

There is real progress. The first wild fledge happened in 2003 in Grand Canyon National Park, and since then 74 condors have hatched in the wild between Arizona and Utah. Thirty years ago, only 29 condors lived in the wild; as of last year, 392 did—though the species is still critically endangered. “This is a very old species,” said program director Tim Hauck. “They survived the last ice age. Condors are resilient.” From the moment the doors opened, it took just 49 minutes for all four birds to take to the skies.
pool.whyMatters: Thirty years of patient work has grown the wild condor population from 29 to 392.

pool.title: Meet the 20 new MacArthur Fellows, from a sea-ice scientist to a saxophonist who cooks onstage
pool.summary: The MacArthur Foundation named 20 new fellows, each receiving a no-strings-attached $800,000 grant. This year’s class spans climate scientists, chemists, historians, poets, visual artists and a 29-year-old jazz saxophonist.
pool.summaryLong:
The MacArthur Foundation has named 20 new recipients of its no-strings-attached, $800,000 fellowship grants, popularly known as “genius grants,” NPR reports via GPB. As usual, the winners, selected through the foundation’s network of scouts, come from a wide range of disciplines.

Several are working on climate and food. Kaiyu Guan, a climate scientist at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, combines satellite data and machine learning to boost food productivity while reducing environmental impacts, including digital platforms that simulate how crops might respond to future weather, water availability and land management. Marika Holland, at the National Center for Atmospheric Research in Boulder, Colorado, studies how polar sea ice interacts with global climate. Holly Jean Buck, a University at Buffalo sociologist, examines the ethics of climate policy and argues carbon removal should serve local communities.

Others are opening new paths in health and chemistry. UC San Diego engineer Liangfang Zhang pioneered cloaking synthetic nanoparticles in natural cell membranes so they can deliver drugs and neutralize toxins without being rejected by the immune system. Stanford organic chemist Song Lin has shown how simple electrical currents—even from a couple of AA batteries—can replace expensive, toxic heavy metals to build complex molecules for medicine. University of Chicago physicist Vincenzo Vitelli uses topology to model how forces move through living tissue, informing understanding of growth and wound healing.

The arts are well represented. Christine Sun Kim, a Berlin-based artist born deaf, makes large charcoal drawings that combine musical notation with American Sign Language grammar to make ASL’s nuances visible to non-signers. Texas painter Vincent Valdez depicts everyday working-class people, particularly from Chicano communities. Santa Fe poet Layli Long Soldier, novelist Bryan Washington and novelist Maaza Mengiste are also honored, along with Zürich-based choreographer Trajal Harrell.

The youngest fellow is 29-year-old New York saxophonist and composer Immanuel Wilkins, who turns concert venues into multisensory spaces—once performing alongside a chef cooking onstage, with chopping, boiling and frying folded into the music. The oldest, at 69, is Flagstaff, Arizona, visual artist Chip Thomas, whose 36 years as a primary care physician on the Navajo Nation inform his work. Historians, economists, a philosopher and a forensic anthropologist round out the class.
pool.whyMatters: Twenty creative people get five years of freedom to pursue work that helps us see and live better.

pool.title: MIT engineers build a paper-thin robot that swims a maze powered by a single layer of muscle cells
pool.summary: An MIT team led by Ritu Raman made a gum-stick-sized gel robot whose two fins are coated with light-sensitive muscle cells. Flashing light on either fin steers it, and it swam and swiveled through a simple watery maze.
pool.summaryLong:
Swimming takes a lot of muscle, but MIT engineers have found that even a single layer of muscle cells can power through water if designed right. In a paper in Advanced Functional Materials, the team presents a thin, muscle-powered swimming robot whose gel “skeleton” is about the length and width of a stick of gum. Each half forms a fin covered with a layer of live muscle cells thinner than a strand of hair, genetically engineered to twitch in response to light.

Shining light on one fin makes it flap with enough force to pull the robot through water; flashing either fin at different intervals controls direction and speed. The bot swam and swiveled through a simple maze in a petri dish. At its fastest it covers about four body lengths per minute—a snail’s pace next to Olympic swimmers, but on par with the leisurely cow shark. “The robot’s quite strong, given its size,” said Ritu Raman, associate professor of mechanical engineering. MIT says it is the first very thin, two-dimensional, muscle-powered robot capable of locomotion.

Most biohybrid robots use bulky 3D chunks of lab-grown muscle requiring millions of cells. Thinner designs could be cheaper and more efficient. The key was optimizing the skeleton. The team swapped ultrasoft fibrin for a stiffer gel called gelatin methacrylate, stamped it with square-bottomed grooves that helped cells align and fuse into strong fibers, settled on a half-millimeter-thin film, and even “exercised” the muscles with a light-flashing training routine.

“You can think of the robot as having two independent muscles,” Raman said. “If we shine a light on just one, only that muscle moves.” Next the team wants to improve the body design for faster swimming. Raman believes muscle-powered robots could one day explore environments too fragile for conventional hardware, “because living tissue is soft, responsive to its surroundings, and can heal itself,” and imagines uses like environmental monitoring in water. First author is Maheera Bawa.
pool.whyMatters: Soft, living robots could someday gently explore places too delicate for metal machines.

pool.title: OHSU becomes first in Oregon to use vagus-nerve implants to help stroke and arthritis patients heal
pool.summary: Neurosurgeons at Oregon Health & Science University are the first in Oregon to implant small FDA-approved devices on the vagus nerve to promote healing. One device helps the brain rewire after stroke; the other aims to calm the inflammation behind rheumatoid arthritis.
pool.summaryLong:
Neurosurgeons at Oregon Health & Science University have reached a medical milestone: they are the first in Oregon to implant small devices on the vagus nerve to promote healing. The vagus nerve is the longest cranial nerve in the body, and the FDA-approved devices send small, precisely targeted electrical impulses along it to the brainstem. Patients barely feel the signal.

“This will be life-altering treatment for a lot of patients,” said Ahmed Raslan, M.D., chair of neurological surgery in the OHSU School of Medicine. “It opens up a new era in bioelectronic medicine.”

For stroke rehabilitation, a thumb-size device is implanted under the skin of the chest with a wire to the left vagus nerve, in an outpatient procedure—people go home the same day. “By stimulating the vagus nerve, you stimulate new synapse connections in the brain,” said neurosurgeon Adam Lipson, M.D., who performed OHSU’s first two stroke cases on Sept. 4. “You’re assisting the brain to reorganize and supplant the pathways that were damaged by the stroke.”

Both of those first patients hope to get back to horses. Lauren Vogel, 47, of La Center, Washington, is walking again after a 2023 stroke but still lacks function in the fingers of her left hand—a major problem since she is left-handed. She envisions returning to work as a horse trainer. “Nothing’s guaranteed, but we’re hopeful and I’ll definitely put the work in,” she said. Stacey Leah Melvin, 58, of Eagle Point in Southern Oregon, wants to be able to help her 18-year-old son, including handing him a brush or holding his horses when he shows them.

For rheumatoid arthritis, OHSU is the first in the Pacific Northwest to offer the treatment. Raslan implanted a vitamin-sized wireless device in the neck, connected to the left vagus nerve. Brooke Braun, 48, of Wilsonville, one of the first patients on Aug. 25, has had arthritis since age 23 and was glad to receive the treatment close to home; it is too early to know whether it helps.

Rheumatologist Cong-Qiu Chu, M.D., Ph.D., explained that the vagus nerve normally senses an immune overreaction and signals the immune system to calm down. Stimulating it “may benefit patients who aren’t responsive to available medications,” he said, describing the device as a complementary therapy.
pool.whyMatters: Oregon patients can now get bioelectronic therapies for stroke recovery and arthritis close to home.

pool.title: An orphaned gorilla returned to the wild has become a mother, a first for her species
pool.summary: Lulingu, rescued as an 18-month-old from the illegal wildlife trade, was one of four eastern lowland gorillas rewilded into Virunga National Park in late 2024. She has given birth to an infant fathered by a wild silverback, and both are healthy.
pool.summaryLong:
One of the first eastern lowland gorillas ever successfully returned to the wild gave birth on May 21 in Virunga National Park in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Good News Network reports—a historic first for the species’ conservation.

The mother, Lulingu, was one of four female gorillas moved at the end of 2024 from the GRACE sanctuary in North Kivu province to Virunga. Her baby was fathered by a wild silverback living on Mount Tshiaberimu, a sign she has integrated into the wild population. Rescuers recovered Lulingu when she was just 18 months old after she was taken from her family and sold into the illegal wildlife trade; she was the youngest orphan ever brought to GRACE, the only sanctuary in the world for rescued eastern lowland gorillas. There, a gorilla named Pinga became her surrogate mother.

The release of the four females—Lulingu, Mapendo, Ndjingala and Isangi—capped a more-than-five-year rewilding process led by GRACE, Virunga National Park and local communities, with support from Gorilla Doctors and Re:wild. The birth also advances a central goal: a genetic boost for the small, isolated gorilla population on Tshiaberimu.

Monitors have tracked the group closely, even collecting urine from leaves and using human pregnancy tests to detect pregnancy hormones. “None of the 4 females have required veterinary treatment for illness or injury since being rewilded,” said Gorilla Doctors veterinarian Dr. Cedric Kibengo. “Both mother and infant are healthy and doing well.” Ranger Benoit Ishaba said the team has seen Lulingu “nursing, cradling, and playing with the baby.”

“This is a milestone for the gorillas,” said Katie Fawcett of GRACE Gorillas, adding the team is cautiously optimistic. At least one other rewilded female may also be pregnant. “Each healthy infant represents more than an addition to the population—it is a sign of resilience, recovery, and what is possible,” said Re:wild’s Mary Brown.
pool.whyMatters: A rescued orphan is now raising the next generation of a critically endangered gorilla.

pool.title: Three shoebox-scale NASA spacecraft launch to test new thrusters, UV astronomy and satellite inspection
pool.summary: Three NASA-supported small spacecraft rode a SpaceX rideshare out of Vandenberg on Oct. 1. One tests a safer, higher-performing propellant, one is NASA’s first astrophysics CubeSat for a hard-to-see band of ultraviolet light, and one will inspect inactive satellites.
pool.summaryLong:
Three NASA-supported small spacecraft launched at 11:32 a.m. PDT on Thursday, Oct. 1, aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 from Space Launch Complex 4 East at Vandenberg Space Force Base in California, part of the company’s Transporter-18 commercial rideshare mission. Together they aim to demonstrate new propulsion technologies, study how galactic dust and high-energy radiation move through galaxies, and advance capabilities for inspecting inactive satellites.

The ASCENT Propulsion Dual Mode CubeSat will demonstrate two forms of propulsion from one shared tank. A single chemical thruster handles maneuvers that need more power, while four electrospray thrusters perform lower-power operations. Both run on ASCENT (Advanced Spacecraft Energetic Non-Toxic), a low-toxicity propellant that is safer to handle during spacecraft processing and has 50 percent higher specific impulse density than conventional propellants like hydrazine. NASA’s Marshall Space Flight Center leads the mission with MIT, Georgia Tech and Rubicon Space Systems.

The SPRITE CubeSat, developed and operated by the University of Colorado Boulder’s Laboratory for Atmospheric and Space Physics and funded by NASA’s Astrophysics Division, will be NASA’s first astrophysics CubeSat to detect a specific range of ultraviolet light that cannot be observed from the ground. About the size of a shoebox—13.5 inches long by 9 inches wide and high—it uses highly sensitive detectors, specialized mirror coatings and an innovative telescope design that could match some much larger instruments. Over a one-year mission it will observe star-forming regions and the remnants of exploded stars in and near the Milky Way, offering insight into how radiation cleared the opaque, neutral gas that fogged up the early universe.

The third mission, SSPICY (Small Spacecraft Propulsion and Inspection Capability), has Starfish Space operating its Otter 24C spacecraft to inspect up to four inoperable U.S.-origin satellites in low Earth orbit. Using new propulsion, autonomous guidance and computer-vision navigation, plus an articulating robotic boom for directing thrust, it will gather information about the objects’ surface condition, geometry and orbits. The mission is expected to run about two years, with inspections beginning in 2027, helping NASA and industry understand how spacecraft could eventually service or help dispose of objects in orbit.

NASA says commercial rideshares like this let science and technology demonstrations share a rocket with other spacecraft, creating more opportunities to test emerging capabilities economically. Its CubeSat Launch Initiative selected the ASCENT demonstration in 2024 and SPRITE in 2021.
pool.whyMatters: Small, affordable spacecraft are testing safer fuel, new UV astronomy and ways to deal with dead satellites.
