pool.title: Volunteers move about 22,000 young salmon and steelhead out of drying Rogue River creeks
pool.summary: The Rogue River Restoration Council and its volunteers rescued roughly 22,000 juvenile steelhead and coho this summer through their Fry Salvage program. They carried fish from shrinking, disconnected tributary pools into the main Rogue River.
pool.summaryLong:
In Southern Oregon, the Rogue River Restoration Council (3RC), a nonprofit serving the Rogue River Basin, rescued approximately 22,000 juvenile steelhead and coho salmon this past summer through its Fry Salvage program, KOBI-TV NBC5 reported.

Juvenile salmon, called fry, typically migrate out of the Rogue’s tributary streams into the main river over the summer. But Oregon’s severe drought and climbing temperatures dried some streams earlier in the season, leaving fish with nowhere to go—an issue that was more pronounced than ever after this year’s uncharacteristically dry weather.

With the help of volunteers, 3RC relocates fish from disconnected, rapidly disappearing streambeds into the Rogue River itself.

“On what was historically one of our Class 1 streams, if we didn’t do some salvage work, every single one of the fry would’ve dried up. So, you basically would’ve taken one of our most productive spawning tributaries and lost a whole generation of fish,” said Scott Howell, president of 3RC.

Howell is clear-eyed that preserving salmon will take expansive, long-term solutions around weather and water use. He describes the group’s work as “a crutch to help our native fish limp along in those streams until there is an answer.”

3RC hopes to continue and expand the effort next summer, and invites volunteers through its website.
pool.summaryLongNote: The source is a short local TV report; this summary sticks to what it says.
pool.whyMatters: Hands-on volunteers saved a whole generation of fish in at least one key spawning creek.

pool.title: A NASA ocean satellite turns out to be able to watch most irrigation canals, UW researchers find
pool.summary: University of Washington researchers found NASA’s SWOT satellite can measure water levels in more than 85% of roughly 800,000 km of Asian irrigation canals, despite never being designed for waterways that small. It could help farmers plan around droughts.
pool.summaryLong:
Irrigation canals are a kind of circulatory system for global agriculture, yet many farming regions have no good way to monitor water flowing through them, relying on scattered gauges and inspections. A new University of Washington study, published Sept. 30 in Geophysical Research Letters, suggests the tools for broad monitoring may already be in orbit.

The Surface Water and Ocean Topography (SWOT) satellite, a joint NASA and international mission in orbit since December 2022, uses interferometric radar to track surface water at least once every three weeks. Its designers assumed canals—often narrower than 20 meters—would be invisible to it. Professor Faisal Hossain wasn’t so sure. In 2025, he and colleagues published GRAIN, a global dataset that used open-source mapping and machine learning to chart 3.8 million kilometers of canals. Lead author Mridul Sharma, a UW graduate research assistant, overlaid SWOT data on that map.

“It was quite the accidental and pleasant discovery to see that SWOT is able to track flow direction and water levels in most of the canals skillfully,” Sharma said. “GRAIN mapped where canals are. SWOT revealed what was happening inside them.”

Across roughly 800,000 km of canals in 22 Asian countries—a region where irrigation helps feed about 3 billion people—the team rated 37.5% of kilometers highly observable, 46.9% moderately and 15.6% poorly, checking their confidence scores against real canal measurements in the U.S. Dense vegetation was the biggest obstacle, and performance should improve as algorithms get better.

UW researchers are already building tools for water delivery in South Asia and canal management in the western U.S. A rice farmer could see that not enough water will arrive and switch to a less thirsty crop like corn or wheat. “Some of the most important scientific discoveries happen when a tool designed for one purpose unexpectedly reveals something else,” Hossain said. “What was once invisible is becoming measurable.”
pool.whyMatters: An existing satellite could help farmers worldwide stretch water and prepare for drought.

pool.title: Tigst Assefa runs the third-fastest women’s marathon ever in Berlin as Guye Adola sets a personal best
pool.summary: At the Berlin Marathon on Sept. 27, Ethiopia’s Tigst Assefa won in 2:11:04, a course record and the third-fastest women’s time in history, despite a late Achilles injury. Her training partner Guye Adola won the men’s race in a personal best of 2:02:50.
pool.summaryLong:
Tigst Assefa came within sight of the women’s marathon world record at the BMW Berlin Marathon on Sunday, Sept. 27, and still won in 2:11:04—the third-fastest time in history, World Athletics reports. Her training partner Guye Adola completed an Ethiopian double, winning the men’s race in a personal best of 2:02:50.

Assefa’s pace was relentless and remarkably even. She ran 10-kilometer sections of 30:48, 30:46, 30:41 and 30:45, hitting halfway in 1:04:57—the third-fastest halfway split ever in a women’s marathon—and reached 40 km in 2:03:00, still projecting a 2:09:44 finish against the world record of 2:09:56. Then she began limping; it later emerged she had suffered a partial tear of her Achilles tendon. With a lead of more than five minutes, she made it to the Brandenburg Gate and across the line, taking 49 seconds off the course record and personal best of 2:11:53 she set in Berlin in 2023. It was her third Berlin win. Ethiopia’s Bedatu Hirpa (2:16:53) and Dera Dida (2:16:55) completed the podium.

The men’s race stayed packed much longer, with nine men together at halfway in 1:01:01. Adola moved to the front by 30 km and made the decisive move soon after, opening a gap by 35 km that only grew. His 2:02:50 took almost a minute off the personal best he set on his marathon debut in Berlin in 2017, when he finished second to Eliud Kipchoge.

It completed a perfect marathon season for Adola, who also won in Rotterdam in April, and gave him a second Berlin title. Gemechu Dida (2:03:19) and Tanzania’s Gabriel Geay (2:03:59) were second and third.
pool.whyMatters: Two training partners delivered a remarkable double win through grit and steady pacing.

pool.title: Oregon Zoo earns another five years of top national accreditation
pool.summary: The Association of Zoos and Aquariums renewed the Oregon Zoo’s accreditation for five more years, announced at AZA’s annual conference in Portland. The zoo was one of the first two in the world accredited, in 1974, and has kept that status ever since.
pool.summaryLong:
The Oregon Zoo has earned another five years of accreditation from the Association of Zoos and Aquariums, KTVZ reports. The announcement came during the association’s annual conference, which this year took place in Portland.

AZA is a nonprofit that accredits 255 zoos and aquariums globally. To earn accreditation, facilities go through a detailed application and a multi-day onsite inspection by zoological professionals who evaluate animal care and well-being, veterinary care, staff training, education programs, conservation efforts, financial stability, risk management, governance and guest services.

“AZA’s standards continuously evolve to reflect best practices in the zoo and aquarium profession, with a strong emphasis on animal care and well-being at their core,” said Dan Ashe, AZA’s president and CEO. “Oregonians can be very proud of their zoo. It ranks among the top zoos nationally and it doesn’t just keep pace. It’s a leader in helping to set our ever-rising standards.”

Zoo Director Heidi Rahn said the review panel singled out something local: “One of the things called out at our accreditation hearing was the incredibly strong community support for this zoo. We will never take that lightly and we are committed to continuous improvement.”

The Oregon Zoo and the Philadelphia Zoo were the first two institutions in the world to earn AZA accreditation, in 1974, and both have held it continuously since. Over the past 15 years, the Oregon Zoo has earned 15 major annual AZA awards, including six for conservation work on behalf of endangered species, two for exhibit design, one for education, one for environmental efforts in daily operations, one for diversity and three for marketing, alongside a Half-Century Award for 50 years of continuous accreditation.

The zoo also received an honorable mention in AZA’s scientific poster competition: animal health director Dr. Carlos Sanchez was recognized with Oregon State University’s Dr. Jennifer Johns and Laura Nutter for research on the role of elephant white blood cells in disease processes.
pool.summaryLongNote: The source is a brief news report; this summary stays within it.
pool.whyMatters: Portland’s zoo keeps meeting rising standards for animal care, five decades running.

pool.title: A town of fewer than 250 people raises $76,000 and builds its own park in a year
pool.summary: In Chelsea, Iowa, local banker Rob Fattig set out to raise money for a community park on an empty lot between the library and a church. Forty-nine sponsors and a crew of volunteers beat the $72,000 goal, adding a bigger shelter and a swing set.
pool.summaryLong:
About two years ago, Rob Fattig—a South Tama County alum who returned to his hometown of Chelsea, Iowa, and took a job at the local bank—started raising funds for a true community park on the green space between the library and Chelsea United Methodist Church on Station Street. This fall, that dream became reality, the Times-Republican reports.

The original goal was to raise $40,000 in the first year toward a total project cost of $72,000. Instead, the community raised the full amount and then some—$76,000—in just one year. The project drew 49 sponsorships, including $10,000 grants from the Mansfield Foundation and the Tama County Community Foundation and five personal and business contributions of at least $5,000. Proceeds from the annual Chelsea Car Show also helped substantially.

The park includes brand-new equipment, a soft rubber mulch surface and a shelter with benches. The extra money paid for a larger shelter and a swing set. “We raised a lot more money than we thought, so we were able to put it to good use,” Fattig said.

It was a true town effort. Before the project, the lot was completely empty. A local farmer donated all the dirt, and excavator and county supervisor Curt Kupka donated the trucking. Local carpenters built the shelter, a concrete supplier donated half the materials, an equipment company from Grimes installed the playground, Alliant Energy added a security light, and other volunteers pitched in. Fattig joked that at times he had more offers to help than work to hand out.

A father of two, he has been blown away by how many kids use the park after school. “It’s really nice to see that small towns can still thrive and still do something,” he said. “Yes, we get flooded, but there’s still things going on in Chelsea.”
pool.whyMatters: A tiny town proved neighbors can pool what they have and build something lasting.

pool.title: Fourteen years in, NASA’s Curiosity rover drills its 48th rock on Mars
pool.summary: Curiosity has successfully drilled its 48th rock target in Gale crater, a spot nicknamed “Basque Lakes” in a newly entered map area called Cache Creek. Despite tight power and an aging rover, the team squeezed in extra science while the sample went to the rover’s onboard labs.
pool.summaryLong:
NASA’s Mars rover Curiosity has successfully drilled into its 48th rock target in Gale crater, a site nicknamed “Basque Lakes,” according to the mission’s team blog, written by Lucy Thompson, a senior research scientist at the University of New Brunswick in Canada.

Before landing, the area of Gale crater the team planned to explore was divided into rectangular parcels, or quads, named after small towns associated with significant geological features; targets within them get unofficial names based on each quad’s theme. Curiosity long ago climbed above the original quads during a 14-year, 38-kilometer (24.6-mile) trek that has included more than 1 kilometer of elevation gain.

The rover recently entered the new Cache Creek quad, named for a geologically diverse area of British Columbia with oceanic crust, marine sediments, volcanic rocks, glacial deposits and lakes with unusual chemistry that may resemble lakes that once existed on Mars. It also lies at the southern end of the 1860s Gold Rush Trail. “While we may not literally strike gold, we are all eagerly anticipating the outcome of the CheMin X-ray diffraction analysis of our drilled sample,” Thompson wrote.

Before drilling, the team used the APXS instrument to measure the rock’s chemistry, brought the MAHLI camera within 1 centimeter (about 0.4 inches) to examine textures, and fired ChemCam’s laser at the target. Engineers checked the rock’s stability with a pre-load test. Despite significant power constraints and an aging rover, they also imaged surrounding terrain with Mastcam, analyzed a nearby bedrock target called “Peace River,” examined the new drill hole and tailings, looked at a jumble of blocks at the base of a butte called “Cordillera,” and kept monitoring the crater’s weather and atmosphere.

The sample was set to go next to the SAM instrument. Curiosity was expected to stay about another week before dumping the sample and driving on to keep exploring Mount Sharp.
pool.whyMatters: A 14-year-old rover is still doing careful, creative science on another planet.

pool.title: Oregon State chemists make a carbon-capture material that keeps working in steamy smokestack gas
pool.summary: Oregon State scientists have filed a patent application for BVR-X, a metal-organic framework that sorts water and carbon dioxide into different parts of its pores. That lets it keep capturing CO2 in very humid flue gas, a problem that defeats many similar materials.
pool.summaryLong:
Oregon State University scientists have filed a patent application for a new carbon capture material that turns the water in factory flue emissions from a problem into an advantage. The work, published in Angewandte Chemie, involves metal-organic frameworks, or MOFs.

MOFs are crystalline materials made of metal ions linked by organic molecules into a repeating, cage-like structure with nanosized pores that soak up gases like a sponge. There are millions of possible MOFs; more than 100,000 have been synthesized. “MOFs have shown a lot of promise because of their porosity and their structural versatility,” said Kyriakos Stylianou, professor of chemistry, who directs OSU’s Materials Discovery Laboratory, the MaD Lab.

Industry accounts for 30% of total U.S. greenhouse gas emissions, according to the EPA. Capturing carbon dioxide at the source, such as a smokestack, is comparatively well developed, but water complicates it: many promising MOFs lose effectiveness in humid, real-world flue gas, and drying the gas adds enough cost to make it nonviable.

The new MOF, dubbed BVR-X, directs water and carbon dioxide to different regions inside its pores, so water doesn’t block the spots where CO2 is captured. “Our new material does something unusual: It responds to water by changing in a way that lets it keep capturing CO2 effectively even under very humid conditions,” Stylianou said. In tests it efficiently captured carbon dioxide from a highly humid stream containing just 4% CO2—conditions relevant to natural gas combustion. “And the material can be regenerated and reused, maintaining performance through dozens of capture-and-release cycles,” he added.

Collaborators included MaD Lab members Ankit Yadav, Emmanuel Musa and Andrzej Gładysiak, OSU College of Engineering researchers, and scientists from UC Berkeley, the University of Oregon and the ARAMCO Research and Development Center. Funding came from Saudi Aramco, the Murdock Charitable Trust and a donor-advised fund of OSU alumni and retired teachers Brian and Marilyn Kleiner.
pool.whyMatters: A reusable sponge that tolerates humidity could make capturing factory CO2 more practical.

pool.title: 1,000-year-old pottery from Georgia’s Etowah Mounds holds the earliest known chocolate east of the Mississippi
pool.summary: Genetic analysis of feast pottery from the Etowah Indian Mounds near Atlanta found cacao DNA dating to around the 11th century. The find suggests trade and kinship networks stretched from the U.S. Southeast toward Central America a millennium ago.
pool.summaryLong:
Chocolate may have helped fuel celebrations by the builders of earthen monuments in Georgia a thousand years ago. A genetic analysis of residues on pottery from near the Etowah Indian Mounds has revealed the earliest known traces of cacao east of the Mississippi River, Smithsonian Magazine reports, expanding archaeologists’ understanding of how goods and ideas spread across the ancient Americas. The study was published Aug. 26 in PLOS One.

Etowah, just northwest of Atlanta, has six earthen monuments built by Native Americans during the Mississippian period; the tallest once rose about 64 feet. Completing a mound was likely celebrated with a large feast. In the 1950s, archaeologists found the remains of such a feast from between 1050 and 1150 C.E. in a borrow pit—a hole dug for red clay and later refilled—and stored the washed pottery sherds for decades.

About a decade ago, University of South Carolina archaeologist Adam King and colleague Terry Powis got permission from the Muscogee people, who hold Etowah sacred, to analyze the residue. They found caffeine in all 31 sherds tested, but couldn’t tell whether it came from cacao or the native yaupon holly, used for tea in the region. Teaming up with French researchers for genetic analysis, they have now reported cacao DNA in two sherds. Its degradation was consistent with a millennium of age, not modern contamination. “I thought they did a really great job,” said University of Arizona archaeologist Barbara Mills, who was not involved.

Cacao grows in tropical lowlands such as southern Mexico, so how it reached Georgia is unclear: a traveler may have brought it directly, or it passed from person to person—possibly via Chaco Canyon in New Mexico, where cacao residue has also been found, or along the Gulf Coast or through the Caribbean and Florida. Dried beans keep a long time, so whoever brought them probably brought a recipe too.

For King, the find shows how connected the Americas were. Kinship and trade networks “were much broader and much more connected than we think they were,” he said. “This is really an Americas story.”
pool.whyMatters: A tiny trace of chocolate reveals how far ancient American communities reached each other.

pool.title: Google launches Guided Vision, a talking camera helper for blind and low-vision Android users
pool.summary: Google rolled out Guided Vision in Gemini Live on Android, letting people share their camera and hear real-time descriptions of their surroundings. It was trained with the visual-interpreting service Aira and tested by more than 1,000 members of Aira’s tester network.
pool.summaryLong:
On Oct. 1, Google launched Guided Vision in Gemini Live across compatible Android devices, bringing voice-forward, real-time visual interpretation to people who are blind, have low vision, or simply want intuitive visual help. The company says the feature was developed in close collaboration with the accessibility community.

To train Gemini Live for real-world conversation, Google partnered with Aira, a visual-interpreting service, on tens of thousands of hours of interpretation data. More than 1,000 members of Aira’s Trusted Tester network stress-tested and refined the model across daily routines, while Aira specialists worked with Google’s teams to help set and evaluate safety guardrails.

With Guided Vision on, users share their camera in a Gemini Live session and hear clear descriptions, ask follow-up questions and get proactive spoken cues. If the camera is pointed too high, too close or off to the side, Gemini prompts them to pan slowly right, tilt down or step back. Google lists everyday uses: reading small nutrition labels, appliance dials and menus in dim restaurants; finding a dropped earbud or the black pepper in a crowded spice cabinet; checking whether a striped shirt goes with a pair of trousers; and getting an overview of an unfamiliar room. It supports multiple languages, reflecting testing with blind and low-vision communities in India, Brazil, Singapore, Indonesia, Japan and elsewhere.

It’s designed to be quick to reach: a toggle in the Gemini app, an Android accessibility shortcut (floating button, two-finger swipe or both volume keys) or the TalkBack menu via a three-finger tap. Google notes it can also help older adults, people with low literacy or anyone reading fine print in low light.

Google is explicit about limits: Guided Vision can make mistakes, is not a medical device or white-cane replacement, and isn’t meant for navigation or obstacle detection. It is available on Android 9 and above where Gemini Live is supported.
pool.whyMatters: Everyday tasks like reading labels get easier for people who are blind or have low vision.

pool.title: Oregon State researchers help build a nationwide network of hourly pollen monitors
pool.summary: Pollen is one of the least-measured common exposures in the U.S., often with one counting station per metro area or none. OSU and University of Washington researchers have placed 43 automated monitors across seven metro regions, reporting hourly counts for nine pollen groups.
pool.summaryLong:
More than 80 million Americans battle sneezing, itchy eyes, runny noses or trouble breathing from pollen, and pollen seasons are lengthening and intensifying with climate change. Yet pollen is one of the least-measured common environmental exposures in the United States, Oregon State University’s College of Health reports.

“Pollen can be a serious health concern, including triggering asthma attacks, which makes it important to have accurate monitoring,” said Assistant Professor Matthew Bozigar. “Currently, networks to measure allergens are sparse. With a single counting station per metro area, and sometimes none, ‘pollen exposure’ in a health study usually means data from the nearest monitor recorded, however far away.”

To fill that gap, Bozigar, Professor Perry Hystad, Assistant Professor Andrew Larkin and undergraduate Samson Naleway have teamed with the University of Washington’s Department of Environmental & Occupational Health Sciences to build a denser network as part of the REACH-SPIROMICS study. So far, 43 automated outdoor pollen monitors have been placed across seven U.S. metro regions—Ann Arbor, Baltimore, Los Angeles, New York, Salt Lake City, San Francisco and Winston-Salem—reporting hourly concentrations for nine priority pollen groups: seven tree categories plus grass and ragweed.

Since early March the group has logged more than 2,695 monitor-days and over 67,605 monitor-hours of data, with more monitors coming online. The team hopes to place 50 new monitors each year for at least two years. Today’s national monitor density is about one per 100,000 square kilometers; other countries have reached about one per 5,000, and the researchers would like a much denser network in Oregon, the Pacific Northwest and nationwide.

“Lack of granular, systematic pollen data collection is a huge bottleneck for understanding its health effects,” Bozigar said; the project aims to study pollen’s role in COPD, for example. The article also shares practical tips for allergy season: keep windows shut, take off shoes indoors, change clothes after being outside, vacuum weekly, wash bedding in hot water and use HEPA air purifiers.
pool.summaryLongNote: Based on a short university feature; this summary stays within it.
pool.source: Oregon State University College of Health
pool.whyMatters: Better local pollen data could help millions of allergy and asthma sufferers breathe easier.

pool.title: A 65-year-old gardener grows a world-record 2,856.8-pound pumpkin in his first solo season
pool.summary: Ian Paton of Lymington, England, set a new world record at the Wargrave Nursery weigh-off on Oct. 3 with a 2,856.8-pound pumpkin. It was his first season competing without his twin brother, and he now has grown the three heaviest pumpkins ever recorded.
pool.summaryLong:
A British gardener has once again set a world record for the largest pumpkin ever grown, The Independent reports. Ian Paton, 65, claimed the title at the Wargrave Nursery Giant Pumpkin Weigh-off in Berkshire on Saturday, Oct. 3, with a 2,856.8-pound (1,295.8 kg) specimen—roughly the weight of a female hippopotamus.

It was his very first season competing without his twin brother, Stuart, who retired his shears to travel. Over five decades the brothers grew five of the 10 heaviest pumpkins in history and won three world titles and 10 European championships together; their previous record-breaker, in 2025, weighed 2,819.8 pounds. Now Paton has grown the three heaviest pumpkins ever recorded.

He knew this one was special when the telehandler lifting it triggered its overload alerts. “I knew it was a big one as when I lifted it with the telehandler, all the warning lights came on like a Christmas tree, saying it was too heavy,” he said.

The work was immense: “It’s five or six hours of work every day for two months. It’s nice to know I can do it myself. A lot of that work is burying the vines so it gets more roots—that’s where the size comes from. The pumpkin grows about a foot and a half or 40cm a day in every direction.”

His granddaughters, Etta, 5, and Martha, 7, helped cheer him on. “The grandkids were amazed. I put it on a WhatsApp call to them when I won and you could hear them shouting down the phone,” he said. And despite the friendly rivalry with growers abroad, he says the hobby has a gentle spirit: “It’s a very friendly sport and everyone works together, so it’s not like other sports.”
pool.whyMatters: Two months of daily, patient gardening produced the heaviest pumpkin on record.

pool.title: Idaho brings the Guinness record for the largest serving of French fries home: 1,474 pounds
pool.summary: At Potato Days at the Idaho Botanical Garden, the Idaho Potato Commission and Spud Daddy served 1,474 pounds of fries, beating a 2018 record from India by more than 20 pounds. About 50 to 60 volunteers helped cut and flash-freeze roughly 1,700 pounds of potatoes.
pool.summaryLong:
Idaho is now home to a new Guinness World Records title after the Idaho Potato Commission and Spud Daddy served up more than 1,400 pounds of French fries on Friday night, Oct. 2, KIVI reports.

The team was aiming to beat the previous record for the largest serving of French fries, which stood at 1,452.85 pounds and was set in India in 2018. “Idaho should have that record,” said Thomas Watson of Spud Daddy. “Idaho doesn’t have that record, and it’s our mission to bring the record home.”

The attempt took plenty of preparation and a large group of volunteers. Watson said about 50 to 60 people helped cut and flash-freeze the potatoes before they were loaded into a refrigerated truck and eventually fried. About 1,700 pounds of raw Idaho potatoes went into the effort. “It’s been awesome just to see it,” he said.

After the fries were cooked and weighed, the final total came in at 1,474 pounds—more than 20 pounds above the previous record—making Idaho the new record holder.

The attempt was part of Potato Days at the Idaho Botanical Garden in Boise, a family-friendly event celebrating Idaho’s potato industry and the farmers, packers, distributors and retailers behind it. It also featured the Big Idaho Potato Truck, live music, lawn games and plenty of potato food, from tots and mashed potatoes to loaded baked potatoes and potato soup.

Once the record was official, Watson was ready to relax: “I’m ready to take a nap… We can go to sleep. We can get some food. We can eat some French fries.”
pool.summaryLongNote: The source is a short local TV report; this summary stays within it.
pool.whyMatters: Dozens of volunteers turned a community potato festival into a world record.

pool.title: More than 1,500 SOLVE volunteers clear nearly 9,000 pounds of litter from Oregon beaches and rivers
pool.summary: SOLVE’s annual Beach & Riverside Cleanup ran 96 projects across 15 counties in Oregon and Southwest Washington from Sept. 18 to 27. In Bend, 42 volunteers picked up 175 pounds of trash along the Deschutes at the Old Mill District.
pool.summaryLong:
More than 1,500 volunteers joined together across Oregon and Southwest Washington for SOLVE’s annual Beach & Riverside Cleanup, completing 96 environmental restoration projects between Sept. 18 and Sept. 27, KTVZ reports. Participants contributed more than 3,100 hours of service across 15 counties during the 10-day campaign.

Volunteers gathered nearly 9,000 pounds of litter and debris from watersheds, beaches and shorelines, keeping it from flowing into the Pacific Ocean. They also cleared 9,450 square feet of invasive plants and mulched 300 plants to help habitat recover.

In Central Oregon, the Pick It Up, Bend! event returned for its second year on Sept. 27 at the Old Mill District, where 42 volunteers collected 175 pounds of trash from popular recreation areas along the river. It was paired with the Johnson Ohana Foundation, linking the morning volunteer work with musician Jack Johnson’s local concert.

Along the coast, organizers hosted 25 cleanups from Astoria and Warrenton down to Gold Beach, where the local group Paws for Nature combined its event with a community dog walk. Inland, volunteers in Southern Oregon joined Bear Creek Stewardship Day across Ashland, Talent, Phoenix and Medford, removing trash, pulling invasive plants and tending pollinator gardens.

“Every year, Beach & Riverside Cleanup shows what is possible when people unite to care for the places they call home,” said SOLVE CEO Kris Carico. “These local efforts add up to a meaningful regional impact.” Projects spanned Clackamas, Clark, Clatsop, Coos, Curry, Deschutes, Jackson, Lane, Lincoln, Marion, Multnomah, Polk, Tillamook, Washington and Yamhill counties.
pool.whyMatters: Thousands of volunteer hours kept tons of trash out of Oregon’s rivers and ocean.

pool.title: A restored carriage road reopens around New York’s Lake Awosting, completing a full lakeside loop
pool.summary: After a 17-month, $1.3 million project, the Lake Awosting Carriage Road at Minnewaska State Park Preserve reopened Sept. 28. Hikers can now loop the entire shore of the largest sky lake on the northern Shawangunk Ridge.
pool.summaryLong:
The Lake Awosting Carriage Road Trail at Minnewaska State Park Preserve in New York’s Shawangunk Mountains has reopened, the Daily Freeman reports. New York State Parks, the Palisades Interstate Park Commission and the Open Space Institute announced the reopening on Monday, Sept. 28, after a 17-month repair project on 2.6 miles of trail along the lake that cost $1.3 million. A $500,000 grant from the state’s Environmental Protection Fund helped make it possible.

Completing the project lets visitors hike a loop around the full perimeter of Lake Awosting, the largest sky lake on the northern Shawangunk Ridge. The work widened and resurfaced sections of the carriage road to accommodate a range of users and extended its lifespan with new retaining walls and drainage improvements that reduce flooding and erosion.

The numbers are impressive: 8,500 linear feet of ditching, 50 culverts, 6,000 square feet of retaining walls, and more than 15,000 tons of road materials installed, graded and compacted. The work was done by Keith Kortright and Keith Kortright Jr. of Mombaccus Excavation.

“Minnewaska State Park Preserve’s carriage road network offers a magnificent way to experience the beauty of the Shawangunks,” said Joshua Laird, executive director of the Palisades Interstate Park Commission. “The reopening of Awosting Carriage Road is another step toward the restoration of the entire network.”

Open Space Institute CEO Erik Kulleseid added that caring for the park “requires long-term commitment from many stakeholders.” The effort advances a goal to rehabilitate all 35 miles of Minnewaska’s Victorian-era carriage roads, which have been eroded by a century of visitor use and weather.
pool.whyMatters: A century-old trail is rebuilt to last, and hikers can circle the whole lake again.

pool.title: Three rehabilitated loggerheads return to the sea, bringing the South Carolina Aquarium to 499 releases
pool.summary: Hundreds of people gathered at Folly Beach County Park as loggerheads Honey, Hope and Buffalo went back to the ocean after months of care. They were the South Carolina Aquarium’s 497th, 498th and 499th sea turtle releases.
pool.summaryLong:
Hundreds of people gathered at Folly Beach County Park in South Carolina as loggerhead sea turtles Honey, Hope and Buffalo returned to the ocean after successful rehabilitation at the South Carolina Aquarium, WCBD reports.

The aquarium says the three were its 497th, 498th and 499th sea turtle releases, bringing it even closer to a long-awaited 500th. All three turtles had been hooked by fishermen and each had its own challenges during rehabilitation. After many months of care, they were cleared for release.

“As Honey, Hope and Buffalo made their way into the surf, cheers rose from community members and Aquarium staff alike who had gathered to celebrate their release,” the aquarium said, adding that there was plenty of excitement for the 500th release just on the horizon.

Who will be number 500 remains a mystery: every patient heals on its own timeline, so the milestone turtle won’t be known until it is deemed ready to go home.

“Just like Honey, Hope and Buffalo—and the hundreds of sea turtles before them—the 500th release will undoubtedly reflect the compassion of our incredible community that comes together time and again to give these turtles a second chance,” said Melissa Ranly, manager of the aquarium’s Sea Turtle Care Center.

The aquarium says sea turtle rehabilitation wasn’t part of its original plan; it grew organically from a turtle in need, a willingness to answer the call and a community that believed in the work.
pool.summaryLongNote: The source is a short local TV report; this summary stays within it.
pool.whyMatters: Hundreds of hooked and injured turtles have been nursed back and sent home.

pool.title: University of Oregon biologists find three new species of brittle star plankton off the Oregon coast
pool.summary: Working from the Oregon Institute of Marine Biology in Charleston, UO researchers Nicole Nakata and Richard Emlet discovered three new brittle star species in coastal plankton. They also photographed and described about 10 larval forms never documented before.
pool.summaryLong:
Nearly every morning as a doctoral student, Nicole Nakata would cross the street from the University of Oregon’s Oregon Institute of Marine Biology (OIMB) in Charleston to the Pacific’s high-tide line, catching microscopic brittle star larvae from the incoming current to study under a microscope. “These larvae are so beautiful and complex, but they are microscopic,” she said. “If you spend time in the ocean, it’s probable you’ve swallowed many larvae.”

Working for years with marine biologist Richard Emlet, her former doctoral advisor, Nakata helped discover three new species of brittle star plankton off the Oregon coast and publish detailed descriptions of about 10 larval species that had never been photographed or described. The work, funded by a National Science Foundation grant and supported by several dozen undergraduate assistants, was published in the June 2026 issue of Invertebrate Biology. “We’d go bananas whenever we found a new species,” Emlet said.

Because larvae often look nothing like adults, the team matched genetic signatures of larval samples to known adults—a step called DNA barcoding. That led to surprises: larval versions of brittle stars whose adults were only known to live hundreds of miles away in British Columbia and the San Francisco Bay Area, showing Oregon’s coastal ecosystems are connected to the wider West Coast. Learning that these species spawn in winter also gives a baseline for conservation. “If we don’t know how something makes babies, we can’t do anything about it,” Nakata said.

The researchers also found some larvae skip developmental stages entirely: mothers produce eggs large enough to nourish larvae through early development without eating, so they go straight to the juvenile stage. “We found a goldmine of examples,” Emlet said. “We had no idea it was happening here in Oregon.”

Nakata now teaches at the University of Alaska Southeast in Juneau. Emlet continues at OIMB and plans to study how larval patterns change during El Niño winters, after noticing some species appeared only in samples from past El Niño events. “We wouldn’t have noticed that if we had not been at OIMB on the coast 24/7,” he said. “We sampled daily.”
pool.whyMatters: Patient daily sampling on the Oregon coast revealed new species and hidden links along the West Coast.

pool.title: A 12-year-old’s fifth annual diaper drive fills a U-Haul with 30,000 diapers for a Phoenix food bank
pool.summary: Twelve-year-old Sloan set out to collect 22,500 diapers this year for Nourish Phoenix, the food and clothing bank where she first volunteered. By the end of her fifth annual drive she had gathered 30,000, delivered by the truckload.
pool.summaryLong:
Employees at a food bank in Phoenix were left scratching their heads when an entire U-Haul truck of donated diapers arrived—knowing that a middle-schooler was behind the enormous load, Good News Network reports.

It was the haul from 12-year-old Sloan’s fifth annual “Diaper Drive,” an event she has organized since she was 7. This year she set a target of 22,500 diapers. Yet the Huggies, Pampers and Blueys kept pouring in until there was hardly room to walk around her house. By the end of the drive she had collected 30,000 disposable diapers for Nourish Phoenix, a food and clothing bank.

The idea started years ago when Sloan volunteered there. While stocking food parcels, she noticed a section of shelves was bare. When she asked why, she was told that was where the diapers went—they were always among the most requested items, and they had already run out.

“If we have the ability to give someone something that they might not have or need, it’s really important to do that,” she told ABC 15 as this year’s drive wrapped up at the end of August.

“My little girl: she’s just so special, she has such a big heart, loves helping and giving back,” said her proud mother.
pool.summaryLongNote: The source is a short feature; this summary stays within it.
pool.whyMatters: A kid noticed an empty shelf and spent five years filling it for local families.

pool.title: Great Smoky Mountains’ storm-damaged John Messer Barn is rebuilt the old-fashioned way
pool.summary: Great Smoky Mountains National Park and Friends of the Smokies finished a full reconstruction of the historic John Messer Barn in Greenbrier, celebrated with a ribbon-cutting on Sept. 28. Builders used traditional techniques, wooden pegs instead of nails, and reused the barn’s original doors.
pool.summaryLong:
Great Smoky Mountains National Park, in partnership with Friends of the Smokies, has completed a full reconstruction of the historic John Messer Barn in the park’s Greenbrier area after extensive storm damage. Park leaders, Friends of the Smokies and descendants of the Greenbrier community celebrated with a ribbon-cutting ceremony on Sept. 28.

The Messer Barn is the oldest structure in Greenbrier and the only building there that predates the park. Multiple storms had severely damaged it, making it unsafe for visitors. The reconstruction used traditional techniques and materials similar to the original construction, including hand-hewn-looking logs, wooden studs in place of nails and the careful preservation and reuse of the barn’s original doors.

The barn is a classic double-cantilever design, a style unique to East Tennessee, and is among the many park structures listed on the National Register of Historic Places. It was built by Pinkney Whaley and later sold to John Messer.

“Preserving historic buildings like the John Messer Barn helps the park honor and share the stories of the many people who called the Smokies home before it became a national park,” said Superintendent Charles Sellars.

Friends of the Smokies funded the work through its Forever Places endowment. “The Messer Barn stands as a powerful reminder of the families, farms and way of life that once made up this mountain community,” said Dana Soehn, the group’s president and CEO. “Thanks to the generosity of our donors, this $465,000 investment ensures this special piece of Smokies history remains a part of these mountains for generations to come.”

Descendants of the Messer family attended the ceremony, sharing stories of parents and grandparents who lived on the property before the park was established. The barn sits one mile up Porters Creek Trail.
pool.summaryLongNote: Based on the park’s brief announcement.
pool.whyMatters: Donors and craftspeople saved the oldest building in Greenbrier for future hikers.

pool.title: OHSU and UW secure $4.6 million to bring clinical research to rural Northwest clinics
pool.summary: OHSU’s Oregon Rural Practice-based Research Network and the University of Washington’s WWAMI-region partners won $4.6 million in renewed CARE for Health funding. It supports two new rural studies: doula support for families and ear acupressure as a non-drug option for chronic pain.
pool.summaryLong:
Researchers at Oregon Health & Science University’s Oregon Rural Practice-based Research Network (ORPRN) and their partners at the University of Washington School of Medicine’s WWAMI region Practice and Research Network have secured $4.6 million in renewed CARE for Health funding, OHSU News reports. The goal is to bring promising clinical studies to rural communities, which are often left out of research.

The 36-month award supports the networks’ role as one of six regional hubs in the national CARE for Health initiative, called the Primary Care Rural and Frontier Clinical Trials Innovation Center, or PRaCTICe. These hubs help people in rural and frontier areas access leading-edge research and evidence-based treatments in their own primary care clinics.

“This work is about making sure rural communities are represented in research and have access to interventions that could improve health outcomes where people live,” said ORPRN director Melinda Davis, Ph.D. “Historically, many clinical trials have been conducted primarily in urban settings.”

One new project will adapt a doula intervention previously focused on Black mothers in urban health systems for rural primary care in the Northwest, based on an NIH-funded trial at the Medical College of Wisconsin. “There is a strong body of evidence demonstrating that doula care leads to improved perinatal outcomes,” said OHSU School of Nursing faculty member Ellen Tilden, Ph.D. “We hope this study will generate evidence that can inform broader adoption of doula services in rural communities where maternity care options are increasingly limited.”

The second joins a national trial led by the University of Texas Health Science Center on auricular point acupressure, in which tiny seeds placed on points of the ear give ongoing pressure patients can self-administer. ORPRN will help enroll patients at rural clinics in Oregon and Wyoming. “This study brings access to a non-drug treatment for chronic pain that would otherwise not be available to rural residents,” said UW’s Sebastian Tong, M.D.

Since first receiving CARE for Health funding in 2024, ORPRN has helped rural clinics join multiple studies. The award comes from the National Institutes of Health.
pool.whyMatters: Rural Oregonians get a fairer shot at joining studies and trying new care close to home.

pool.title: An 11,000-drone show over Texas sets two Guinness World Records
pool.summary: Over three nights in Blue Ridge, Texas, Sky Elements and Damoda America flew 71,207 drones across seven shows, a Guinness record for one week. The finale used 11,000 drones, and a 10,183-drone dragon set a second record.
pool.summaryLong:
U.S. drone show company Sky Elements has set two Guinness World Records titles after flying more than 71,000 drones across seven shows over three consecutive nights in Blue Ridge, Texas, DroneDJ reports. The run included an 11,000-drone performance the company says is the largest drone show ever flown in America.

Working with Damoda America, Sky Elements launched a total of 71,207 drones in one week, beating the previous record of 55,939. An official Guinness World Records adjudicator was on site to verify the flights. The shows ran from Sept. 27 through Sept. 29: six performances with more than 10,000 drones each, followed by the 11,000-drone finale.

The team also set a record for the largest aerial display of a mythical creature, using 10,183 drones to draw a giant dragon in the Texas sky—smashing the previous mark of 2,247.

The performances featured a rotating cast of giant formations, including an eagle, a lion, a dragon and Pegasus, along with turning gears, Americana-inspired imagery and scenes from deep space. The finale moved through recreations of Noah’s Ark and a black hole before closing with a UFO sequence.

Pulling off multiple 10,000-plus drone flights on successive nights wasn’t just a matter of putting more drones in the air: crews had to recharge and relaunch the fleet between performances while pilots, engineers and designers coordinated on site. CEO Rick Boss said shows at this scale have traditionally been associated with Asia and the Middle East, and the Texas event aimed to show American operators can deliver them at home.

DroneDJ notes the industry has steadily moved from small novelty displays toward elaborate alternatives to fireworks.
pool.summaryLongNote: Based on a short trade-news report and the company’s announcement of the verified records.
pool.whyMatters: A crew pulled off seven giant, verified sky shows in three nights—fireworks-free spectacle.

pool.title: North Tulsa celebrates a new 33,000-square-foot Rudisill Library in the historic Greenwood District
pool.summary: The new Rudisill Regional Library opened Saturday, Oct. 3, at 1017 N. Greenwood Ave. in Tulsa. It adds a maker space, podcast studio, teen center, expanded African American Resource Center and art by Tulsa artist Dell Chambers.
pool.summaryLong:
The new Rudisill Regional Library is now open in Tulsa’s historic Greenwood District. Members of the Tulsa City-County Library Commission, elected officials and community members celebrated Saturday with a ribbon cutting and a full day of events at the 33,000-square-foot facility at 1017 N. Greenwood Ave., the Tulsa Flyer reports.

“Greenwood has always been a place where people turn ideas into opportunity, where knowledge passed from one generation to the next and where community was a source of strength,” said Kimberly Johnson, CEO of the Tulsa City-County Library. “What an incredible place for a public library to call home.”

The new Rudisill features a maker space, a podcasting studio, event space, an outdoor patio, a teen center and expanded space for the African American Resource Center. It also includes pieces by Tulsa artist Dell Chambers reflecting “the history, people and spirit of Greenwood,” along with artifacts discovered during construction.

Regional manager Keith Jemison began his career shelving books under Freddie Rudisill, the branch’s first manager. After the ribbon cutting he said he was “very much on cloud nine.” “I feel very much connected to the ancestors, previous librarians and everyone who has used the library and what it has meant in their lives,” he said. “Bring your little ones and let them have that lifetime experience here. There’s something for everyone.”

Rudisill is one of four libraries the system is relocating and expanding through its MY Library, OUR Future capital campaign, which officials said raised nearly $54 million. Johnson said a library “must be a bridge between generations and a doorway to opportunity.” It is open daily, with weekday hours from 9 a.m. to 9 p.m.
pool.summaryLongNote: The source is a short local news report; this summary stays within it.
pool.whyMatters: A neighborhood gains a bigger, free place to learn, make things and gather.

pool.title: Two Oregon State geoscientists, including a South Sister volcano expert, named to North America’s “50 Under 50”
pool.summary: OSU ecohydrologist Pam Sullivan and incoming associate professor Christy Till were named to the Geological Society of America’s 50 Under 50 list for mid-career excellence and mentorship. Till was nominated by 12 alumni of her lab.
pool.summaryLong:
Pam Sullivan, the Hollis M. Dole Professor in Geosciences in Oregon State University’s College of Earth, Ocean, and Atmospheric Sciences (CEOAS), and Christy Till, who joins CEOAS as an associate professor in January, have been named to the Geological Society of America’s 50 Under 50 list, OSU Today reports. The award, a collaboration among geological societies of the U.S., Canada and Mexico, highlights outstanding mid-career scientists in North America who are also active in service and mentorship.

“I remember looking at the list and thinking, ‘Wow, these are really cool people,’” Sullivan said. “It’s nice for people to say, ‘We think you’re doing a good job.’” Her ecohydrology research ranges from how roots take up water in soil to how whole watersheds function and how wildfire, new vegetation and chemistry affect water—even the hardness of residents’ tap water. She’s working on a proposal to use AI to make global water-data aggregation more efficient, and runs a summer camp bringing undergraduates to Kansas for hands-on fieldwork.

Mentorship shaped her own path. “I was probably not a person who most people would’ve thought would be successful in science, because I had some pretty strong learning disabilities,” she said. “Giving people the opportunity to explore science in ways that interest them is really important because you never know what’s going to come of it.”

Till, coming from Arizona State University, will teach volcanology at OSU. She uses the chemistry of past eruption deposits to reconstruct the life story of a volcano’s magma and what triggered eruptions. One of her main subjects is Oregon’s South Sister, ranked the seventh-highest eruption threat in the U.S., where the causes of past eruptions are relatively unknown. She also makes small amounts of magma in lab experiments and will build a lab at OSU to do that.

Till calls mentoring students the most rewarding part of her job, and found the honor especially meaningful because 12 alumni from her lab nominated her. “I feel very fortunate to be recognized for my hard work thus far in this way,” she said.
pool.whyMatters: Two scientists who study Oregon’s water and volcanoes are honored for research and mentoring.

pool.title: A UMass Amherst wrist wearable tracks stroke recovery all day, so therapy can adapt in real time
pool.summary: UMass Amherst researchers built a wrist device with an accelerometer and machine-learning model that continuously estimates arm impairment after stroke. In their study, it reflected patients’ condition 40–50% more accurately than standard clinician evaluation.
pool.summaryLong:
A team led by University of Massachusetts Amherst researchers has developed a wearable wrist device, powered by a machine-learning algorithm, that can continually track changes in arm-movement impairment caused by strokes. The goal is to let clinicians adjust therapy in real time for personalized care instead of today’s one-size-fits-all standard. The work, with colleagues from Washington University in St. Louis, Shirley Ryan AbilityLab and Harvard Medical School/Mass General Brigham, is described in Science Translational Medicine.

More than 795,000 Americans have strokes each year, and upper-limb mobility problems affect up to 77% of patients right afterward; about 40% have chronic issues. Progress is usually measured by a roughly 30-minute clinician assessment, so it typically happens only before and after rehabilitation. “During that therapy process, neither the patient nor the therapist has a clear idea of how patients are responding,” said corresponding author Sunghoon Ivan Lee, an associate professor in UMass Amherst’s Manning College of Information and Computer Sciences.

The device’s accelerometer captures upper-limb movement throughout the day in patients’ real lives, and an algorithm developed by Lee and lead author Ryan Wang interprets it. Trained on accelerometer data and clinician scores from subacute stroke patients and healthy people, the model was 40–50% more accurate—a better reflection of the patient’s true condition—than clinician evaluation. “We are the first group to actually show that, using wearable data, we can extract information about patients’ motor severity, which clinicians can actually use,” Lee said. Patients who can see their own progress may also stay more motivated.

It helps research too: recreating a previous study with the digital biomarker produced statistically significant results with 50% fewer participants, which could speed studies and cut costs.

The work was supported by the National Institutes of Health. With a provisional patent filed, Lee is pursuing commercialization through the startup Lumid Health, and partners are recruiting stroke patients for a study at Spaulding Rehabilitation Hospital in Boston.
pool.whyMatters: Stroke survivors and therapists could see recovery progress every day, not just twice.

pool.title: More than 650 endangered mountain yellow-legged frogs hop back into Southern California streams
pool.summary: In August, the Aquarium of the Pacific, Los Angeles Zoo and U.S. Geological Survey released more than 650 captive-raised southern mountain yellow-legged frogs at two sites in the San Gabriel Mountains. It is part of a 20-plus-year effort to keep one of the region’s rarest amphibians on the landscape.
pool.summaryLong:
Frog release days start at about 4 a.m., so staff can reach the site before the heat, said Erin Lundy, manager of conservation initiatives at the Aquarium of the Pacific. The first challenge is catching the frogs: a newly morphed southern mountain yellow-legged frog is about an inch long, fast and very good at squeezing into cracks, Mongabay reports.

In August, the aquarium, the Los Angeles Zoo and the U.S. Geological Survey released more than 650 of the endangered frogs at two sites in the San Gabriel Mountains—nearly 400 of them reared at the aquarium. This year’s cohort arrived as 2-month-old tadpoles bred at the L.A. Zoo; through winter and spring, staff watched their limbs emerge and tails reabsorb. Head-starting frogs through metamorphosis in captivity boosts their odds of survival. After a two-hour drive, the team hiked past waterfalls and deep pools and floated the containers so the frogs could acclimate before setting them free.

“One time, a frog jumped out of the container, landed on a rock, and immediately ate a fly … And I was like … We’ve done it. He’s functional,” Lundy said.

The frogs were once so abundant in Southern California’s mountains that biologists had trouble walking without stepping on one. Declines began in the 1950s with non-native trout, and habitat loss, climate change and the chytrid fungus followed; a 2023 survey counted fewer than 200 frogs in the southern population. Captive breeding began as a salvage operation in 2003, when 10 frogs were rescued after a wildfire and taken to the San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance. The L.A. Zoo, breeding them since 2007, has bred and released more than 7,000.

Researchers are exploring antifungal treatments, immune priming and drier release sites where frogs can bask off the fungus. There is room for hope: in the Sierra Nevada, a related frog has recovered after reintroductions of chytrid-resistant parents. “Reintroduction, having the ability to start new populations, is really essential for the persistence of the species,” said SDZWA researcher Talisin Hammond. In September, Lundy picked up about 500 new tadpoles: “They’ve been eating so much already in the last few days, so I think this is going to be a good year for our tadpoles,” Lundy said.
pool.whyMatters: Zoo and aquarium teams are rebuilding a nearly lost frog population one release at a time.

pool.title: Oregon State welcomes 400-plus science writers to Corvallis for ScienceWriters2026
pool.summary: Oregon State hosted the ScienceWriters2026 conference Sept. 25–28, bringing more than 400 science journalists and communicators to campus. Close to 100 OSU researchers took part, and visitors toured places from the Hatfield Marine Science Center to the Bread Lab and OSU Creamery.
pool.summaryLong:
Oregon State University hosted the ScienceWriters2026 conference Sept. 25–28, bringing more than 400 science journalists and communicators to the Corvallis campus to meet OSU researchers and see their work firsthand, OSU Today reports. It was the organizers’ first conference on the West Coast since 2017 and the first in the Pacific Northwest since 2007. The event is run by the National Association of Science Writers and the Council for the Advancement of Science Writers.

Corvallis weather cooperated, and attendees took breaks outdoors to soak in the sunshine. The weekend opened with visits to the OSU Radiation Center, the Emmerson Advanced Wood Products Laboratory and the under-construction Jen-Hsun Huang and Lori Mills Huang Collaborative Innovation Complex. On Monday, attendees fanned out on nine trips, including to the Hatfield Marine Science Center in Newport, the College of Pharmacy in Portland, McDonald-Dunn Research Forest, the O.H. Hinsdale Wave Research Lab, the veterinary teaching hospital, the Research Brewery, the Bread Lab, the Research Winery and the OSU Creamery.

Close to 100 OSU researchers took part, representing nearly every college, and more than 30 faculty hosted “Lunch with a Scientist” tables. OPB’s Jes Burns hosted a live “All Science. No Fiction” show, and local Grass Roots Books sold titles by Pacific Northwest authors and attending writers. More than 40 university volunteers, including students interested in science communication, staffed the event.

“This was a rare opportunity to bring the media world to Corvallis to see our labs and meet our experts,” said Misty Edgecomb, director of OSU Media Relations, noting the team was already working with reporters on eight news stories. Conference manager Skylar Gunderson-Erhardt said many attendees called it one of the best conference experiences they’d had: “By the end of the conference, many attendees were already saying they wished the conference could return to OSU every year.”
pool.whyMatters: Hundreds of science storytellers met Oregon researchers, seeding more science news for everyone.
